Fix test.\n\n**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.\n\n### GREEN - Minimal Code\n\nWrite simplest code to pass the test.\n\n<Good>\n```typescript\nasync function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {\n  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {\n    try {\n      return await fn();\n    } catch (e) {\n      if (i === 2) throw e;\n    }\n  }\n  throw new Error('unreachable');\n}\n```\nJust enough to pass\n</Good>\n\n<Bad>\n```typescript\nasync function retryOperation<T>(\n  fn: () => Promise<T>,\n  options?: {\n    maxRetries?: number;\n    backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';\n    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;\n  }\n): Promise<T> {\n  // YAGNI\n}\n```\nOver-engineered\n</Bad>\n\nDon't add features, refactor other code, or \"improve\" beyond the test.\n\n### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass\n\n**MANDATORY.**\n\n```bash\nnpm test path/to/test.test.ts\n```\n\nConfirm:\n- Test passes\n- Other tests still pass\n- Output pristine (no errors, warnings)\n\n**Test fails?** Fix code, not test.\n\n**Other tests fail?** Fix now.\n\n### REFACTOR - Clean Up\n\nAfter green only:\n- Remove duplication\n- Improve names\n- Extract helpers\n\nKeep tests green. Don't add behavior.\n\n### Repeat\n\nNext failing test for next feature.\n\n## Good Tests\n\n| Quality | Good | Bad |\n|---------|------|-----|\n| **Minimal** | One thing. \"and\" in name? Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |\n| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |\n| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |\n\n## Why Order Matters\n\n**\"I'll write tests after to verify it works\"**\n\nTests written after code pass immediately. Passing immediately proves nothing:\n- Might test wrong thing\n- Might test implementation, not behavior\n- Might miss edge cases you forgot\n- You never saw it catch the bug\n\nTest-first forces you to see the test fail, proving it actually tests something.\n\n**\"I already manually tested all the edge cases\"**\n\nManual testing is ad-hoc. You think you tested everything but:\n- No record of what you tested\n- Can't re-run when code changes\n- Easy to forget cases under pressure\n- \"It worked when I tried it\" ≠ comprehensive\n\nAutomated tests are systematic. They run the same way every time.\n\n**\"Deleting X hours of work is wasteful\"**\n\nSunk cost fallacy. The time is already gone. Your choice now:\n- Delete and rewrite with TDD (X more hours, high confidence)\n- Keep it and add tests after (30 min, low confidence, likely bugs)\n\nThe \"waste\" is keeping code you can't trust. Working code without real tests is technical debt.\n\n**\"TDD is dogmatic, being pragmatic means adapting\"**\n\nTDD IS pragmatic:\n- Finds bugs before commit (faster than debugging after)\n- Prevents regressions (tests catch breaks immediately)\n- Documents behavior (tests show how to use code)\n- Enables refactoring (change freely, tests catch breaks)\n\n\"Pragmatic\" shortcuts = debugging in production = slower.\n\n**\"Tests after achieve the same goals - it's spirit not ritual\"**\n\nNo. Tests-after answer \"What does this do?\" Tests-first answer \"What should this do?\"\n\nTests-after are biased by your implementation. You test what you built, not what's required. You verify remembered edge cases, not discovered ones.\n\nTests-first force edge case discovery before implementing. Tests-after verify you remembered everything (you didn't).\n\n30 minutes of tests after ≠ TDD. You get coverage, lose proof tests work.\n\n## Common Rationalizations\n\n| Excuse | Reality |\n|--------|---------|\n| \"Too simple to test\" | Simple code breaks. No record, can't re-run. |\n| \"Deleting X hours is wasteful\" | Sunk cost fallacy. Keeping unverified code is technical debt. |\n| \"Keep as reference, write tests first\" | You'll adapt it. That's testing after. Delete means delete. |\n| \"Need to explore first\" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |\n| \"Test hard = design unclear\" | Listen to test. GPT-5.6 supports `none`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, and `max`.\n  - If you are migrating from GPT-5.5 or GPT-5.4, preserve your current reasoning effort as the baseline, then compare one level lower.\n  - If you use `none`, keep it as your latency baseline and also test `low` when the workflow benefits from reasoning or tool use.\n  - Use `medium` as a balanced starting point and `low` for latency-sensitive workloads.\n  - Use `high` or `xhigh` when more reasoning produces a measured quality gain.\n  - Reserve `max` for the hardest quality-first workloads. Compare `max` and `xhigh` to find the best quality, latency, and cost tradeoff for your use case.\n- To use pro mode, keep your selected GPT-5.6 model and set `reasoning.mode` to `pro` in the Responses API; do not switch to a separate Pro model slug. Choose `reasoning.effort` independently. If you omit it, GPT-5.6 defaults to `medium` in both standard and pro modes. See [reasoning mode](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning#reasoning-mode) for a request example and billing details.\n- Configure persisted reasoning based on how much prior reasoning is still relevant. GPT-5.6 models default to `all_turns`; earlier models default to `current_turn`.\n  - Omit `reasoning.context` or set it to `auto` to use `all_turns`, the GPT-5.6 default. Check the response's `reasoning.context` field to confirm the effective mode.\n  - Set `reasoning.context` to `all_turns` when the task's goals, assumptions, and priorities stay stable across turns.\n  - With `all_turns`, continue with `previous_response_id` to make reasoning from earlier responses available to the model.\n  - When managing history manually, preserve and resend previous user inputs and every response output item. For `store: false` or Zero Data Retention, replay the encrypted reasoning items that the API returns by default.\n  - Set `reasoning.context` to `current_turn` when earlier reasoning is no longer relevant.\n- Review prompt caching. You do not need to change code to keep using implicit caching. Because GPT-5.6 cache writes cost 1.25× the uncached input rate, track `cached_tokens` and `cache_write_tokens` to understand net cost. Use explicit breakpoints or `prompt_cache_options.mode: \"explicit\"` to avoid unnecessary writes, and replace `prompt_cache_retention` with `prompt_cache_options.ttl`.\n- To use Programmatic Tool Calling, add the `programmatic_tool_calling` tool and opt eligible tools in with `allowed_callers`. Update your application to handle `program` items, program-issued function calls, and `program_output` items while preserving each call's `call_id` and `caller` linkage. See the [Programmatic Tool Calling guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-programmatic-tool-calling) for request and continuation examples.\n  - Benchmark the PTC-enabled workflow on representative tasks. Compare task success, final-answer completeness, required evidence, total tokens, latency, and cost. Fewer calls, turns, or intermediate outputs are improvements only when the final answer still meets the required quality bar.\n\n## Prompting best practices\n\n### Favor leaner prompts\n\nRemoving repeated instructions and examples and simplifying tool descriptions can improve task performance and token efficiency. In a sample of internal coding-agent eval runs, configurations with leaner system prompts improved evaluation scores by roughly 10–15% while reducing total tokens by 41–66% and cost by 33–67%. Results will vary by workload, so treat these ranges as directional and validate changes on representative tasks from your own application.\n\nTo simplify prompts without losing important guidance:\n\n- Start with a prompt and tool set that already works. Remove one group of instructions, examples, or tools at a time, then rerun the same evals.\n- State each instruction once.\n- Expose only tools relevant to the task, and keep their descriptions concise and precise.\n- Keep examples and style guidance when they encode a product requirement or correct a measured gap.\n- Track context both at the start of a run and as the conversation grows. Long sessions can amplify repeated prompt and tool content.\n\n### Define autonomy and approval boundaries\n\nGPT-5.6 can be proactive and persistent when carrying out multi-step tasks. Define what level of action each request authorizes so the model can continue safe, in-scope work without unnecessary pauses while stopping before external, destructive, costly, or scope-expanding actions.\n\nA compact policy is usually sufficient:\n\n```text\nFor requests to answer, explain, review, diagnose, or plan, inspect the relevant\nmaterials and report the result. Do not implement changes unless the request also\nasks for them.\n\nFor requests to change, build, or fix, make the requested in-scope local changes\nand run relevant non-destructive validation without asking first.\n\nRequire confirmation for external writes, destructive actions, purchases, or a\nmaterial expansion of scope.\n```\n\nName safe local actions explicitly, such as reading files, inspecting logs, editing in-scope code, and running tests. Keep the policy in one place and state each rule once. Repeating instructions such as “ask first,” “do not mutate,” or “wait for approval” can cause unnecessary approval requests for safe, expected actions.\n\n### Set response length and style\n\nGPT-5.6 tends to be more concise by default than GPT-5.5. When migrating, check whether broad brevity instructions such as “Be concise” or “Keep it short” are still useful. They may be unnecessary for some tasks and can sometimes make responses too brief. Keep them when they reliably produce the output your application needs.\n\nFor more consistent control across requests, use `text.verbosity` to set the default level of detail, then use the prompt for task-specific requirements.\n\n#### Set a default with `text.verbosity`\n\nChoose `low`, `medium`, or `high` as the default level of detail for a request. In the prompt, specify any task-specific length, structure, or required content. See [Set up `text.verbosity`](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/deployment-checklist#set-up-textverbosity) for an API example.\n\n#### Specify what a short answer must include\n\nWhen a task calls for a shorter answer, identify the information the model must preserve and the detail it can omit. For example:\n\n```text\nLead with the conclusion. Include the evidence needed to support it, any material\ncaveat, and the next action. Omit secondary detail and repetition.\n\nKeep all required facts, decisions, caveats, and next steps. Trim introductions,\nrepetition, generic reassurance, and optional background first.\n```\n\nThis gives the model a clear priority order: preserve the content needed to complete the task, then remove lower-value detail.\n\n#### Define the tone\n\nBroad labels such as “friendly” or “empathetic” can be ambiguous. Describe the writing choices that define your product's tone, such as how directly to state the answer, when to acknowledge a problem, and whether reassurance or a sign-off is appropriate.\n\n```text\nState the answer directly. If the user reports a problem, acknowledge the\nspecific issue before giving the next step. Use reassurance only when it is\nrelevant. Omit generic praise and unnecessary sign-offs.\n```\n\n### Pro mode\n\n#### Choose pro mode when quality matters most\n\nPro mode is a Responses API execution mode that applies more model work to a request before returning a single final answer. It can improve reliability on difficult tasks, but it increases latency and aggregates the tokens from that work in reported usage. Those tokens are billed at the selected model's standard token rates.\n\nUse pro mode when a marginal quality improvement materially affects the outcome and the task is difficult enough to benefit, such as complex optimization, high-value coding or review, or deep analysis with clear evaluation criteria. Prefer standard mode for routine, latency-sensitive, or high-volume work, and whenever your evaluations do not show a meaningful gain from pro mode.\n\nReasoning mode and reasoning effort are independent. Pro mode works with any GPT-5.6 model and its supported reasoning efforts. Start with the same model and effort as your standard-mode baseline, then compare configurations on representative tasks instead of assuming that the highest effort is always the best tradeoff.\n\n#### Configure pro mode in the API\n\nEnable pro mode in the API request. Keep the same outcome-focused prompt you use in standard mode: state the goal, relevant context, constraints, required evidence, success criteria, and output format. You do not need to ask the model to “use pro mode,” “think harder,” or generate several candidate answers.\n\nFor example:\n\n```text\nReview this database migration plan for failure modes that could cause data loss\nor extended downtime. For each finding, cite the relevant step, estimate impact\nand likelihood, and recommend a specific mitigation. Return the five most\nimportant risks in severity order.\n```\n\n#### Compare quality and cost\n\nCompare standard and pro modes on the same representative tasks. Measure task success, answer completeness, required evidence, total tokens, latency, and cost. Use pro mode selectively where its quality or reliability gain justifies the extra model work.\n\nLearn more in the [reasoning mode guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning#reasoning-mode).\n\n### Programmatic Tool Calling\n\n#### Choose Programmatic Tool Calling by task shape\n\nProgrammatic Tool Calling (PTC) works best for bounded workflows where code can process several tool results or large intermediate outputs and return a much smaller structured result. Use it for filtering, joining, ranking, deduplication, aggregation, validation, or other predictable processing.\n\nMultiple, parallel, or dependent calls alone do not justify Programmatic Tool Calling. Prefer direct, non-PTC tool calls when:\n\n- One call is sufficient\n- The intermediate outputs are already small\n- Each result may change the model’s next decision\n- An action requires approval\n- The final output must preserve citations or native artifacts\n\n#### Make routing instructions task-specific\n\nDo not rely on tool availability or generic instructions such as “use Programmatic Tool Calling efficiently” to produce the right route. When both direct and programmatic calling are available, explicitly state:\n\n- Which bounded stage should use Programmatic Tool Calling.\n- Which tools it may call.\n- The exact output schema and required evidence.\n- Concurrency, retry, and stopping limits.\n- Which work should remain direct.\n\nTool descriptions should document their expected return fields, types, and error behavior. If the model cannot determine the return shape before writing the program, prefer direct tool calling so it can inspect the result before deciding how to use it.\n\nIf both routes are needed, define one clear handoff and tell the model not to switch routes or repeat completed work.\n\nFor example:\n\n```text\n<tool_orchestration>\nUse Programmatic Tool Calling for [bounded stage] using only [eligible tools].\nRun independent calls concurrently when safe. Use only documented tool input\nand output fields.\n\nProcess and reduce the intermediate results, then emit exactly [output schema],\nincluding the evidence needed for the final answer.\n\nStop when [condition] is met. Retry transient failures at most [R] times.\nDo not repeat completed calls or perform side-effecting actions. If a required\nresult is still missing, return a clear structured failure.\n\nUse direct tool calls for [semantic judgment, approval, or final validation].\n</tool_orchestration>\n```\n\n#### Assess the final answer\n\nThe `program_output` item and final assistant `message` are separate outputs; make sure to test both. In theory, a program can return the correct records while the message omits a required field, citation, or caveat.\n\nCompare direct and programmatic calling on the same representative tasks. Check whether the final response is correct, complete, and includes the required evidence. Then compare total tokens, latency, cost, calls, turns, and retries. Count lower resource use as an improvement only when the response still passes your existing evals.\n\nLearn more in the [Programmatic Tool Calling guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-programmatic-tool-calling).\n# Upgrading to GPT-5.6 Sol\n\nUse this guide when the user asks to migrate an existing OpenAI API integration, repository, prompt stack, agent, model router, or model picker to GPT-5.6 Sol or the GPT-5.6 family.\n\nThe default explicit target is `gpt-5.6-sol`. The alias `gpt-5.6` routes to Sol; use it only when the repository intentionally prefers family aliases. <!-- codex-event:{"kind":"progress","timestamp":"2026-08-01T08:05:25.817Z","phase":"commentary"} -->
## Codex progress · 2026-08-01T08:05:25.817Z

I’ve found the first concrete mismatch: the official guidance says `gpt-5.6-sol` is the flagship model, but OmniHarness’s Codex catalog still starts at GPT-5.5 and its Codex defaults still point to GPT-5.4. The warning itself appears to be emitted by the installed Codex runner, so I’m checking whether OmniHarness is launching an older Codex build as well as fixing its stale catalog.

<!-- /codex-event -->

## Codex progress · 2026-08-01T08:15:33.488Z

I’ve confirmed the supported compatibility fix: the old ACP runner accepts a current model catalog when OmniHarness removes only the two reasoning levels that old ACP cannot parse and restores one renamed metadata field. That gives the old runner full GPT‑5.6 Sol limits, tools, instructions, and context information instead of generic fallback data. I’m writing regression tests for that path and for the default/order before changing production code.

Use `@agentclientprotocol/codex-acp`\n> for new installs.\n\nUse [Codex](https://github.com/openai/codex) from [ACP-compatible](https://agentclientprotocol.com) clients such as [Zed](https://zed.dev)!\n\nThis tool implements an ACP adapter around the Codex CLI, supporting:\n\n- Context @-mentions\n- Images\n- Tool calls (with permission requests)\n- Following\n- Edit review\n- TODO lists\n- Slash commands:\n  - /review (with optional instructions)\n  - /review-branch\n  - /review-commit\n  - /init\n  - /compact\n  - /logout\n- Client MCP servers\n- Auth Methods:\n  - ChatGPT subscription (requires paid subscription and doesn't work in remote projects)\n  - CODEX_API_KEY\n  - OPENAI_API_KEY\n\nLearn more about the [Agent Client Protocol](https://agentclientprotocol.com/).\n\n## How to use\n\n### Zed\n\nThe latest version of Zed can already use this adapter out of the box.\n\nTo use Codex, open the Agent Panel and click \"New Codex Thread\" from the `+` button menu in the top-right.\n\nRead the docs on [External Agent](https://zed.dev/docs/ai/external-agents) support.\n\n### Other clients\n\nOr try it with any of the other [ACP compatible clients](https://agentclientprotocol.com/overview/clients)!\n\n#### Installation\n\nInstall the adapter from the latest release for your architecture and OS: https://github.com/zed-industries/codex-acp/releases\n\nYou can then use `codex-acp` as a regular ACP agent:\n\n```\nOPENAI_API_KEY=sk-... codex-acp\n```\n\nOr via npm:\n\n```\nnpx @zed-industries/codex-acp\n```\n\n## License\n\nApache-2.0\napp-server-client\napp-server-daemon\napp-server-protocol-noop-macros\napp-server-protocol\napp-server-test-client\napp-server-transport\napp-server\n"

ONLY THEN: Make the claim\n\nSkip any step = lying, not verifying\n```\n\n## Product-Surface Verification\n\nWhen the work involves an app, UI, or product surface, verification must cover more than whether a single requested feature works.\n\nKeep verification proportional. When client state, server state, cache state, stream state, and persisted state all exist, every plan needs explicit invariants.\n\n## Core Rule\n\nNo UI surface may treat data as authoritative unless the payload proves ownership, freshness, completeness, ordering, and terminal state.\n\nIf those words are missing from the plan, the plan is probably baking in a race condition.\n\n## Planning Checklist\n\nFor every React app that reads server/runtime state, the plan must answer:\n\n1. **Owner:** What owns this state: server, client manager, URL, cache, stream, local storage, or worker/runtime?\n2. **Token:** What owner token protects async results: `requestId`, `runId`, `projectPath`, `operationId`, `workerId + seq`, or equivalent?\n3. **Provenance:** Is data server-authoritative, optimistic, cached preview, partial update, or historical fallback?\n4. **Completeness:** Does the payload declare what scope it is complete for? What may it erase?\n5. **Ordering:** What stable order is used: monotonic seq, `(createdAt, id)`, version, or cursor?\n6. **State machine:** What are the legal states, terminal states, and transitions?\n7. **Events:** Which server decisions are named events rather than client-side derivations?\n8. **Loading shape:** Which states are bootstrap, first load, incremental refresh, reconnect, resync, recovery, and terminal error?\n9. **Fallbacks:** Which legacy/fallback rows can render, and only after what authority is loaded?\n10. **Tests:** Which race, stale-response, event-sequence, reconnect, and merge tests prove the invariants?\n\n## Invariants To Require\n\n- Cached and optimistic data may pre-render, but cannot satisfy full-load gates.\n- Partial snapshots may add or refine state, but may not erase optimistic objects, delivered user input, read markers, or stream entries unless they declare complete scope.\n- Every async response checks that its owner token still matches before mutating visible state.\n- Mutation success handlers may navigate or clear UI only if they still own the current context, unless the action explicitly creates a new selected context.\n- Timers and polling callbacks re-check ownership immediately before acting.\n- Server decisions are emitted as named events; the client does not infer decisions by diffing snapshots.\n- SSE/WebSocket streams have event ids, replay/resume, and an explicit resync path.\n- Loading booleans are split by lifecycle stage. A leaf stream refresh must not unmount the whole page.\n- Append-only content has one writer, one reader, stable ids, and monotonic cursors.\n- Fallback DB rows or historical rows are gated behind stream loading and deduped by stable id plus safe equivalence.\n- Status classifiers distinguish active, runnable, blocked, awaiting user, terminal, stale, and recoverable states.\n- \"Latest\" queries have deterministic tie-breakers. Timestamp-only ordering is not enough.\n- Hot paths use bounded reads and do not synchronously load large bodies, bridge probes, schema setup, or heavy app graphs.\n- Process-local caches have explicit TTL/size bounds and invalidation rules.\n\n## Test Matrix\n\nPick the rows that match the work. Do not rely on one happy-path UI test.\n\n| Risk | Test shape |\n| --- | --- |\n| Stale async response | Start request A, switch owner, resolve A, assert it cannot mutate B |\n| Optimistic object erased | Create local optimistic state, apply stale/partial snapshot, assert object remains |\n| Cache masquerades as loaded | Hydrate cache preview, assert full-load gate waits for server authority |\n| Mutation steals navigation | Start mutation, switch selection, resolve mutation, assert focus stays put |\n| Timer/poll stale-fire | Use fake timers or deferred promises; callback must re-check owner before acting |\n| Snapshot merge erases stream | Apply partial snapshot missing known entries, assert entries/read markers remain |\n| Event stream gap | Bootstrap snapshot, emit events during disconnect, reconnect with last id, assert replay or resync |\n| Server decision invisible | Exercise branch and assert named event such as `blocked`, `refused`, `gave_up`, or `error.surfaced` |\n| State classifier wrong | Table-test every status into active/runnable/terminal/recoverable buckets |\n| Fallback duplicates stream | Load fallback rows then stream entries, assert no duplicate or false chronology |\n| Hot path bloats | Assert snapshots carry cursors not bodies; route returns before DB/heavy imports when possible |\n| Timestamp tie | Insert equal timestamps, assert deterministic order by id/seq |\n\nUse headless HTTP/SSE tests for control-plane decisions. Use React/unit tests for manager merging and ownership guards. Use Playwright only for real UI layout, focus, scroll, mobile computed styles, and visible affordances.\n\n## Refuse These Shapes\n\n- one `isLoading` boolean for bootstrap, refresh, reconnect, and recovery;\n- cache or optimistic data treated as authoritative without provenance;\n- async callbacks that mutate state without checking owner tokens;\n- client-side derivation of server decisions;\n- snapshot diffs used as the only way to know what happened;\n- event streams without ids or resume;\n- timestamp-only \"latest\" queries;\n- parallel transcript or persistence surfaces that the frontend must reconcile;\n- unbounded process caches introduced to hide slow storage;\n- tests that prove only the DOM result when the bug is a server decision.\n\n## Review Prompt\n\nAsk this before implementation starts:\n\n> What can arrive late, out of order, partially, twice, or after the user changes context, and what test proves it cannot corrupt visible state?\n"
  }
]

const patch = "*** Begin Patch\n*** Add File: /Users/masterman/NLP/omniharness/docs/superpowers/learnings/2026-08-01-codex-acp-model-metadata-must-roll-with-codex.md\n+# Codex ACP Model Metadata Must Roll With Codex\n+\n+**Date:** 2026-08-01\n+**Context:** OmniHarness Codex worker startup, model discovery, and ACP installation\n+**Symptom:** Starting a Codex worker with `gpt-5.6-sol` warned that model metadata was missing and fell back to generic metadata.\n+**Root Cause:** OmniHarness installed a June-built Rust ACP fork embedding Codex 0.124. The separately installed Codex CLI and the UI model list could advance, but the ACP process kept its own obsolete model registry. The fork had also drifted far enough from current Codex interfaces that simply changing its dependency tag produced extensive compile failures.\n+**Fix:** OmniHarness now uses the maintained `@agentclientprotocol/codex-acp` adapter, launches it with a separately rolling `@openai/codex` package, and injects the live `codex debug models` catalog into the managed Codex configuration. GPT-5.6 Sol is the default and model discovery respects Codex capability priority. The Unix and Windows installers compare both npm package versions and refresh them together; normal OmniHarness startup already invokes the ensure-only installer. The Docker image and scheduled compatibility workflow use the same official packages.\n+**Verification:** `pnpm typecheck`; `pnpm build`; targeted Vitest coverage for model ordering, metadata compatibility, saved-default migration, supervisor defaults, and installer rolling updates; live `codex debug models` catalog inspection; ACP protocol initialization smoke test; production restart and readiness check. The full suite passed 2,372 tests with two unrelated parallel-run failures that both passed when rerun alone.\n+**Prevention:** Treat the ACP adapter, Codex executable, model registry, and UI catalog as one compatibility surface. Never infer ACP model support from the standalone CLI version alone. Prefer the maintained app-server adapter and remote/live model discovery; keep a tested compatibility transform only for legacy adapters. Any future distribution change must verify the adapter version, Codex version, ACP initialization, and visible model order together.\n+**Skill/Doc Updates:** No general agent skill needed a project-specific rule. The durable system changes are the rolling installers, launcher, Docker image, scheduled compatibility workflow, managed model-catalog bridge, and this project note.\n*** End Patch";
text(await tools.apply_patch(patch));

## Codex final · 2026-08-01T08:52:54.720Z

Fixed and live.

- Root cause: OmniHarness was launching a stale ACP embedding Codex `0.124.0`, so GPT‑5.6 metadata genuinely didn’t exist there.
- Active stack is now `codex-acp 1.1.7` with Codex `0.146.0`.
- GPT‑5.6 order is now: **Sol → Terra → Luna → GPT‑5.5 → GPT‑5.4**.
- `gpt-5.6-sol` is the default. The previous saved default migrates to Sol after reload.
- [tool-env.ts](/Users/masterman/NLP/omniharness/src/server/agent-runtime/tool-env.ts) injects the current live Codex model catalog, preventing metadata drift.
- [install-agent-acp.sh](/Users/masterman/NLP/omniharness/scripts/install-agent-acp.sh) now updates both the maintained ACP adapter and Codex CLI together during normal OmniHarness startup.
- The [rolling compatibility workflow](/Users/masterman/NLP/omniharness/.github/workflows/codex-acp-release.yml) checks current releases weekly.
- Docker and Windows installation paths were updated too.
- Production was rebuilt, restarted, and is ready.

Verification: 118 relevant tests passed, typecheck passed, build passed, live ACP initialization passed, and the live catalog returned Sol first. The full suite passed 2,372 tests; two parallel-run isolation failures passed when rerun individually.

The old 0.124 binary is preserved at `/Users/masterman/.local/bin/codex-acp.legacy-rust-v0.124.0`.

If the request is a tiny mechanical edit, make the edit directly with targeted verification.\n\n## Proportional Skill Use\n\nDo the smallest responsible workflow that matches the request.\n\nFor tiny, unambiguous mechanical edits, do the edit directly:\n\n- changing a color value,\n- fixing a typo,\n- tweaking short copy,\n- changing a prompt sentence,\n- renaming a label,\n- adjusting obvious spacing or formatting,\n- making a one-line config or docs correction.\n\nFor these, do not run brainstorming, write a plan, or force TDD unless the change affects product behavior, data, persistence, control flow, user journeys, or non-obvious architecture.\n\nUse the heavier process when the request is ambiguous, user-facing behavior changes, multiple files/modules are involved, the user journey can change, or the change could create regressions that are not obvious from a quick targeted check.\n\n## Default Posture\n\n- Work in the current repository by default.\n- YOU WILL NEVER CREATE A BRANCH unless explicitly instructed.\n- Ask the user whether we should work in worktrees as part of the planning.\n- YOU WILL ONLY CREATE A WORKTREE if explicitly instructed.\n- Keep skill use proportional. Tiny mechanical edits should stay tiny.\n- Every project should have a `.gitignore`.\n- Never commit or push secrets, credentials, local environment files, `node_modules`, dependency caches, build outputs, coverage output, logs, temporary files, or intermediate/generated artifacts unless the human explicitly asks to version a specific generated artifact.\n- Deliver full product functionality by default. NO FAKE COMPONENTS, NO MOCKS, NO PLACEHOLDERS, NO FALLBACKS as substitutes for the requested functionality unless the human explicitly asks for a prototype or scaffold.\n- For app, UI, and product-surface work, run a PM pass during planning. Treat it as mandatory default behavior, not optional polish.\n- For app, UI, and product-surface work, consider `agentic-user-journey-testing` for important user stories, but do not run it without explicit user approval.\n- Use `second-opinion` for substantial saved implementation plans, and for unusually hard, creative, high-risk, or architecture-heavy specs when an independent external review could improve the artifact. Prefer a different available coding harness for that review, such as Codex asking Claude Code or Claude Code asking Codex. If no different harness is available, the same harness is fine; the second opinion is still mandatory for matching artifacts.\n- Refactor code when a file passes 1200 lines. Do not normalize oversized files as the default end state.\n- Use user stories in specs and plans when they clarify behavior or value.\n- Default UI work to `shadcn/ui` unless the user says otherwise.\n- For any dashboard, admin surface, product UI, SaaS app, internal tool, settings-heavy app, data table view, auth flow, sidebar layout, or React/Next.js web app UI, use `start-from-blocks` before designing or implementing. Start by installing or copying the closest fitting official shadcn Block, then adapt it. No vibed dashboard/web-app design from blank files.\n- Before adding any individual UI control, check whether `shadcn/ui` already provides a control that does what is needed. Use the available shadcn control first, then customize it, instead of hand-building a one-off control.\n- Treat desktop and mobile responsiveness as first-class from the beginning.\n- Prefer explicit routing unless the framework strongly defaults to file-based routes.\n- For React apps, use `building-react-apps` for state managers, explicit transitions, routing, refs, imports, package-manager defaults, and frontend configuration defaults.\n- For React apps with server state, optimistic UI, caches, polling, SSE/WebSocket streams, background jobs, persistence, or client/server synchronization, use `client-server-state-invariants` during planning and verification.\n- For React or Next.js slowness, root-load, compile-time, SSR/hydration, bundle, import-bloat, or UI dependency cleanup work, use `optimizing-react-next-apps`.\n- Prefer strong instrumentation and auditability for backend behavior.\n- When a project has backend or agent workflows, prefer a fully instrumented control plane: persist meaningful events, tool calls, actions, results, errors, and state transitions, and expose them through a CLI or other scriptable interface so the full system can be inspected and tested without the UI.\n- Use `instrumenting-control-planes` when building, planning, reviewing, or debugging backend decisions, agent workflows, recovery paths, retries, deletes, long-running jobs, SSE/WebSocket streams, or user-visible failures.\n- Use `learning-from-bugs` after diagnosing or fixing meaningful architecture, storage, memory, persistence, control-plane, or system-level bugs so reusable lessons become durable.\n- Do not default to silent, masked, or over-abstracted errors.\n- When a project has a frontend, prefer surfacing full backend error details and stack traces to the frontend so failures stay visible, debuggable, and testable end-to-end.\n- Treat persistence of settings and preferences as explicit design work.\n- For every meaningful UI setting, define whether it persists, where it is stored, how it is read and written, who owns it, and how reset, sync, migration, and testing are handled.\n\nSee `docs/ultrapowers-defaults.md` for the canonical fork defaults.\n\n## Skill Priority\n\n1. Process skills first\n2. Implementation skills second\n\nExamples:\n\n- \"Make this button blue\" -> inspect the relevant file, make the small edit, do targeted verification\n- \"Update this prompt sentence\" -> edit the prompt directly and verify the final text\n- \"Build a feature\" -> `brainstorming` with a PM pass first, then `writing-plans`, then execution; consider approval-gated `agentic-user-journey-testing` for app workflows\n- \"Fix this bug\" -> `systematic-debugging`, then the relevant implementation skill; if the root cause is meaningful or systemic, finish with `learning-from-bugs`\n- \"Review this change\" -> `requesting-code-review`\n\n## Examples Of User Override\n\n- If a task feels risky and the user did not ask for extra repository isolation, keep working in the current repository unless the user explicitly instructs otherwise.\n- If a stack supports file-based routing but the user says not to use it, choose an explicit routing approach instead.\n- If a framework strongly defaults to file-based routing, such as Next.js App Router, use the framework-native routing model unless there is a good reason not to.\n- If a frontend skill suggests `shadcn/ui` but the user wants another design system, follow the user.\n\n## Red Flags\n\n- \"I need a whole workflow for this tiny edit\" -> no. Use the smallest responsible process.\n- \"This is simple, so I need the whole process anyway\" -> no. Tiny mechanical edits should stay tiny.\n- \"I'll create extra repository isolation just to be safe\" -> forbidden unless the user clearly asked for it.\n- \"I already know the skill\" -> read the ## Codex final · 2026-08-05T20:30:56.106Z

Yes. End users do not build the ACP adapter from source.

What happens now:

- `./omniharness` automatically runs the [ACP setup check](/Users/masterman/NLP/omniharness/omniharness:174).
- It downloads the published, prebuilt `@agentclientprotocol/codex-acp` and Codex packages.
- It checks npm for newer versions and updates them automatically.
- Manual update command:

```bash
./scripts/install-agent-acp.sh --codex-acp=npm
```

- A [weekly GitHub check](/Users/masterman/NLP/omniharness/.github/workflows/codex-acp-release.yml:1) tests the latest versions on macOS, Linux, and Windows and verifies GPT‑5.6 Sol metadata exists.

I updated everything now:

- ACP adapter: `1.1.9`
- Managed Codex: `0.146.1`
- Standalone Codex: `0.146.1`
- GPT‑5.6 Sol metadata: verified present

One important distinction: the binaries are not literally committed into Git because they are large and platform-specific. They are downloaded prebuilt during normal installation—there is no compilation. An entirely offline installation would need separate platform-specific release bundles.

    "text": "Warning: truncated output (original token count: 15456)\nTotal output lines: 1875\n\n# OmniHarness\n\nOmniHarness is a local control plane for supervising ACP-backed coding agents.\nOne logical headless runner owns SQLite, auth, supervision, PTYs, and agent\nprocesses; the shared Vite interface runs in the web/PWA, Electron, iOS,\nAndroid, and VS Code and can stay connected to multiple runners.\n\nUse it when you want one durable place to start coding-agent runs, watch worker output, recover conversations, inspect execution events, and keep local agent processes behind a clear supervisory layer.\n\n## What You Get\n\n- **Multi-agent supervision:** start implementation, planning, and direct-control conversations with supported ACP workers.\n- **Live run visibility:** stream messages, worker output, execution events, and status changes while a run is active.\n- **Durable local history:** persist runs, messages, workers, settings, auth records, and execution events in SQLite.\n- **CLI parity:** launch and watch the same conversation modes from the terminal.\n- **ACP server mode:** expose OmniHarness itself as an ACP agent over stdio for compatible clients.\n- **Managed agent environment:** spawn workers with a practical `PATH` even when the app starts from a GUI, editor, or service manager.\n- **Phone-friendly local UI:** run the web app as a local PWA for supervising work away from the terminal.\n- **Multi-runner clients:** save any number of authenticated runners, keep their\n  event streams live, and switch the visible workspace without reconnecting.\n\n## Project Status\n\nOmniHarness is early open-source software under active development. Expect sharp edges, fast-moving internals, and occasional database or workflow changes. The core local loop is the priority: reliable worker launch, observable agent activity, durable recovery, and straightforward developer setup.\n\n## Requirements\n\n- macOS, Linux, or Windows with a normal developer shell. On Windows, use PowerShell for the setup commands below.\n- Node.js 22.13 or newer, up to but not including Node.js 26. If you use `nvm`, run `nvm use` from the repo root to select the recommended local version.\n- pnpm 9 or newer. The `packageManager` field in `package.json` is a known-good Corepack default, not an exact-version requirement.\n- `ripgrep` (`rg`) is recommended for fast agent repository search. The `./omniharness` launcher installs it automatically when a supported system package manager is available. Set `OMNIHARNESS_SKIP_RECOMMENDED_TOOLS=1` to skip recommended tool setup.\n- At least one supported coding agent when you want to run real workers:\n  - Codex CLI plus `codex-acp`\n  - Claude CLI plus `claude-agent-acp`\n  - Gemini CLI with native ACP mode\n  - OpenCode with native ACP mode\n- Docker, if you want OmniHarness to run `codex-acp` from a container instead\n  of compiling the Rust adapter on the host.\n\n## Quick Start\n\nClone the repo, enter it, and select the recommended Node version:\n\n```bash\ngit clone <repo-url> omniharness\ncd omniharness\nnvm use\n```\n\nStart OmniHarness normally:\n\n```bash\n./omniharness\n```\n\nOn first start, `./omniharness` asks you to create a web login password. Press\nEnter to have it generate one for you. Generated passwords are printed once in\nthe terminal; save that password before continuing. The launcher stores only an\nArgon2 hash in `.env`.\n\nThe launcher opens [http://localhost:3050](http://localhost:3050) when the local\nserver is ready. Set `OMNIHARNESS_OPEN_BROWSER=0` if you do not want it to open a\nbrowser automatically.\n\n`./omniharness` installs dependencies when needed, builds the static interface\nwhen needed, then starts the two processes in one logical runner deployment:\n\n- the API/SSE server and static interface on `http://localhost:3050`\n- the co-located ACP bridge on `http://127.0.0.1:7800`\n\nStart the runner directly with `pnpm runner`. Use `--no-static` for a supported\nAPI-only deployment, or `--static-dir <path>` for an explicit interface\nartifact.\n\n## Clients and deployment\n\nThe browser/PWA is served by any runner with `dist/interface`. The other hosts\nare remote clients and never embed or start a runner:\n\n```bash\npnpm electron:build\npnpm electron:package:local\npnpm vscode:build\npnpm vscode:package\npnpm mobile:sync\n```\n\nOperational and security details:\n\n- [Runner deployment, data roots, proxies, backup, and smoke checks](docs/deployment/runner-operations.md)\n- [Authentication, sessions, credential storage, identity, and TLS](docs/security/authentication-and-tls.md)\n- [Desktop/editor migration, mobile/PWA limits, and v1 non-goals](docs/platforms/client-migration-and-limits.md)\n\n### Windows Quick Start\n\nUse PowerShell from the repo root. If Corepack can write to your Node.js\ninstallation, enable the repo's package manager normally:\n\n```powershell\ncorepack enable\ncorepack prepare pnpm@11.2.2 --activate\n```\n\nIf Corepack fails with an `EPERM` error under `C:\\Program Files\\nodejs`, install\npnpm into the user npm prefix instead:\n\n```powershell\n$prefix = Join-Path $env:APPDATA \"npm\"\nNew-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $prefix | Out-Null\nnpm config set prefix $prefix\n$env:Path = \"$prefix;$env:Path\"\n[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable(\"Path\", \"$prefix;$([Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable(\"Path\", \"User\"))\", \"User\")\nnpm install -g pnpm@11.2.2\n```\n\nThen clone, install, build, and start:\n\n```powershell\ngit clone <repo-url> omniharness\ncd omniharness\npnpm install\nCopy-Item .env.example .env\n# Set OMNIHARNESS_AUTH_PASSWORD or OMNIHARNESS_AUTH_PASSWORD_HASH in .env.\npnpm build\n$env:OMNIHARNESS_OPEN_BROWSER = \"0\"\npnpm start\n```\n\nThe web UI listens on `http://localhost:3050` and the runtime listens on\n`http://127.0.0.1:7800`. For browser access from another machine, allow inbound\nTCP traffic to the web port in Windows Firewall and in any provider firewall, or\nput OmniHarness behind a tunnel or reverse proxy. Do not expose the runtime port\ndirectly to the public internet.\n\nRun the separate restart control app if you want a small remote escape hatch\nwith its own password-gated interface:\n\n```bash\npnpm restart:control\n```\n\nIt listens on port `3099`. Open `http://localhost:3099` to see status, recent\nlogs, and buttons to start OmniHarness in dev or production mode. The web login\nuses `OMNIHARNESS_AUTH_PASSWORD_HASH` or `OMNIHARNESS_AUTH_PASSWORD` when either\nis configured, then falls back to `OMNIHARNESS_REMOTE_RESTART_PASSWORD`, then to\nthe generated token file.\n\nTo keep the restart controller alive across reboots even when macOS does not\nauto-login, install the boot-time daemon:\n\n```bash\n./scripts/install-restarter.sh\n```\n\nIt installs as a `LaunchDaemon` by default. If you explicitly want the older\nlogin-session `LaunchAgent` behavior, set\n`OMNIHARNESS_RESTART_LAUNCHD_SCOPE=user` before running the installer.\n\nThe script API creates `.omniharness/remote-restart-token` on first run and\naccepts bearer auth:\n\n```bash\ncurl -X POST \"http://HOST:3099/restart?mode=dev\" \\\n  -H \"Authorization: Bearer $(cat .omniharness/remote-restart-token)\"\n```\n\nUse `mode=prod` to launch `./omniharness` instead of `pnpm run dev`.\n\nFor phone access through Cloudflare Tunnel, expose the restart app as a second\nhostname that points to `http://localhost:3099`, for example:\n\n```yaml\ningress:\n  - hostname: horse-battery-staple.omniharness.dev\n    service: http://localhost:3050\n  - hostname: restart-horse-battery-staple.omniharness.dev\n    service: http://localhost:3099\n  - service: http_status:404\n```\n\n## Optional Setup\n\nCreate a local env file only if you want password auth, phone pairing, public-origin links, or API-key based agent/model access:\n\n```bash\ncp .env.example .env\n```\n\nLocal agent CLIs that are already logged in usually work without API keys. If you want the supervisor model or runtime workers to use provider keys from the environment, fill in the relevant variables in `.env`.\n\n## Password Auth\n\nOmniHarness requires a password before the web UI can create an authenticated session or pair a phone.\n\nFor the simplest local setup, run the launcher and follow the prompt:\n\n```bash\n./omniharness\n```\n\nIf `.env` or the current shell already contains `OMNIHARNESS_AUTH_PASSWORD` or\n`OMNIHARNESS_AUTH_PASSWORD_HASH`, the launcher keeps that existing configuration.\n\nChange or reset the password from the repo root:\n\n```bash\npnpm auth:password set\n```\n\nPass the password as an argument when you need a one-line command:\n\n```bash\npnpm auth:password set \"new-password\"\n```\n\nThe command removes active `OMNIHARNESS_AUTH_PASSWORD` and\n`OMNIHARNESS_AUTH_PASSWORD_HASH` lines from `.env`, then writes one fresh\nArgon2 hash. Restart OmniHarness after changing the password.\n\nCheck or test the configured password:[REDACTED] auth:password status\npnpm auth:password verify \"new-password\"\n```\n\nHash-only passwords cannot be printed back out. If `status` says the password is\nhash-only and you do not know it, run `pnpm auth:password set` to replace it.\n\n## Remote Tunnel\n\nFor phone or remote-browser access, expose only the web UI port through your\ntunnel provider. With Cloudflare Tunnel quick tunnels:\n\n```bash\ncloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:3050\n```\n\nCopy the generated `https://...` URL into `.env` and restart OmniHarness:\n\n```bash\nprintf 'OMNIHARNESS_PUBLIC_ORIGIN=%s\\n' 'https://your-tunnel-url' >> .env\n./omniharness\n```\n\nKeep OmniHarness password auth enabled even when your tunnel provider also has\nits own access controls.\n\nThe launcher does not require a global `omniharness` install. Run the app from\nthe checkout with `./omniharness`, and run CLI conversations from the checkout\nwith `./omni`.\n\nPreview the agent adapter setup only when you want to install or refresh\noptional ACP adapters:\n\n```bash\nscripts/install-agent-acp.sh --dry-run\n```\n\nThen run the installer directly when you are ready:\n\n```bash\nscripts/install-agent-acp.sh\n```\n\nThe setup script detects supported local coding agents and installs or refreshes\nthe ACP adapters they need. Codex uses a prebuilt `codex-acp` binary by default\nfor macOS/Linux on arm64/x64 and Windows x64. Claude's adapter is installed from npm, while\nGemini and OpenCode expose native ACP commands and do not need separate adapter\ninstalls. The setup script also checks common agent tools including `rg`, `git`,\n`node`, shell/file utilities, package managers, Python, `jq`, `gh`, `cargo`,\n`uv`, `fd`, and `make`.\n\n### Prebuilt Codex ACP\n\nOmniHarness avoids compiling `codex-acp` with host Rust by default. In `auto`\nmode, the installer downloads the matching release asset:\n\n```text\ncodex-acp-darwin-arm64\ncodex-acp-darwin-x64\ncodex-acp-linux-arm64\ncodex-acp-linux-x64\ncodex-acp-windows-x64.exe\n```\n\nUseful overrides:\n\n```bash\nOMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_INSTALL=binary\nOMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_RELEASE_REPO=danduma/omniharness\nOMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_RELEASE_TAG=codex-acp-latest\nOMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_DOWNLOAD_BASE_URL=https://github.com/danduma/omniharness/releases/download/codex-acp-latest\nOMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_INSTALL_DIR=/custom/bin\n```\n\nOn Windows, use the PowerShell installer to download `codex-acp.exe` into\n`%LOCALAPPDATA%\\OmniHarness\\bin`:\n\n```powershell\npowershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\\install-agent-acp.ps1 -AddToPath\n```\n\nGit Bash/MSYS users can also run `scripts/install-agent-acp.sh`; it installs\nthe Windows release asset as `codex-acp.exe`.\n\nFor local development against the Rust source, force Cargo mode:\n\n```bash\nscripts/install-agent-acp.sh --codex-acp=cargo\n```\n\n### Docker-backed Codex ACP\n\nIf the prebuilt binary cannot run on a machine, install a Docker-backed wrapper\ninstead:\n\n```bash\nOMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_INSTALL=docker ./omniharness\n```\n\n--- LAUNCHER 1 ---\n#!/usr/bin/env bash\nset -euo pipefail\n\nROOT_DIR=\"$(cd \"$(dirname \"${BASH_SOURCE[0]}\")\" && pwd)\"\n\ncd \"$ROOT_DIR\"\n\nAUTH_PASSWORD_NOTICE_FILE=\"\"\n\nprint_auth_password_notice() {\n  if [ -n \"$AUTH_PASSWORD_NOTICE_FILE\" ] && [ -s \"$AUTH_PASSWORD_NOTICE_FILE\" ]; then\n    printf '\\n'\n    cat \"$AUTH_PASSWORD_NOTICE_FILE\"\n    printf '\\n'\n    rm -f \"$AUTH_PASSWORD_NOTICE_FILE\"\n    AUTH_PASSWORD_NOTICE_FILE=\"\"\n  fi\n}\n\ncleanup_auth_password_notice() {\n  if [ -n \"$AUTH_PASSWORD_NOTICE_FILE\" ]; then\n    rm -f \"$AUTH_PASSWORD_NOTICE_FILE\"\n  fi\n}\n\ntrap 'print_auth_password_notice; cleanup_auth_password_notice' EXIT\n\n# --- Ensure a supported Node.js version (>=22.13 <26) ---\n# Native deps (better-sqlite3, @node-rs/argon2, sharp) only build on this range,\n# so if the active Node is outside it, switch via nvm (installing nvm if needed)\n# rather than failing. Set OMNIHARNESS_SKIP_NODE_AUTOINSTALL=1 to opt out.\nMIN_NODE=\"${OMNIHARNESS_MIN_NODE_VERSION:-22.13.0}\"\nMAX_NODE_EXCL=\"${OMNIHARNESS_MAX_NODE_VERSION_EXCLUSIVE:-26.0.0}\"\n\nnode_version_ok() {\n  command -v node >/dev/null 2>&1 || return 1\n  node -e '\n    const cmp = (a, b) => {\n      a = String(a).replace(/^v/, \"\").split(\".\").map(Number);\n      b = String(b).replace(/^v/, \"\").split(\".\").map(Number);\n      for (let i = 0; i < 3; i += 1) {\n        const x = a[i] || 0, y = b[i] || 0;\n        if (x !== y) return x - y;\n      }\n      return 0;\n    };\n    const cur = process.versions.node;\n    process.exit(cmp(cur, process.argv[1]) >= 0 && cmp(cur, process.argv[2]) < 0 ? 0 : 1);\n  ' \"$MIN_NODE\" \"$MAX_NODE_EXCL\" 2>/dev/null\n}\n\nif ! node_version_ok && [ \"${OMNIHARNESS_SKIP_NODE_AUTOINSTALL:-0}\" != \"1\" ]; then\n  echo \"[omniharness] Node $(node --version 2>/dev/null || echo 'missing') is unsupported (need >=$MIN_NODE <$MAX_NODE_EXCL); switching via nvm...\" >&2\n\n  NODE_TARGET=\"22\"\n  [ -f \"$ROOT_DIR/.nvmrc\" ] && NODE_TARGET=\"$(tr -d ' \\t\\r\\n' < \"$ROOT_DIR/.nvmrc\")\"\n  export NVM_DIR=\"${NVM_DIR:-$HOME/.nvm}\"\n\n  if [ ! -s \"$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh\" ] && command -v curl >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n    echo \"[omniharness] Installing nvm into $NVM_DIR...\" >&2\n    curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.40.5/install.sh | bash >/dev/null 2>&1 || true\n  fi\n\n  # nvm.sh is not written for `set -euo pipefail`; relax it while sourcing/using.\n  if [ -s \"$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh\" ]; then\n    set +eu\n    . \"$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh\"\n    nvm install \"$NODE_TARGET\" >/dev/null 2>&1\n    nvm use \"$NODE_TARGET\" >/dev/null 2>&1\n    set -eu\n  fi\nfi\n\nif ! node_version_ok; then\n  echo \"OmniHarness requires Node.js >=$MIN_NODE <$MAX_NODE_EXCL, but the active Node is $(node --version 2>/dev/null || echo 'missing').\" >&2\n  echo \"Auto-switch failed. \"@/server/supervisor/retry\";\n\n--- RUNNER OPERATIONS ---\n# Runner deployment and operations\n\n## Process model\n\nOne OmniHarness runner is one logical deployment with two co-located\nprocesses:\n\n- the API server owns SQLite, auth, supervision, PTYs, settings, files, and the\n  HTTP/SSE contract;\n- the ACP bridge owns agent processes and listens on loopback by default.\n\nClients connect only to the API server. Electron, iOS, Android, VS Code, and\nbrowser/PWA clients never connect directly to the bridge.\n\n`pnpm runner` starts the API server and starts or adopts a loopback bridge. The\nAPI remains available in a degraded state while a failed bridge retries. All\nstart, adopt, retry, refusal, failure, and shutdown choices emit named events.\n\n## Build and start\n\nBuild the shared static interface and start a normal runner:\n\n```bash\npnpm install\npnpm build\npnpm runner\n```\n\nThe default API/UI address is `http://0.0.0.0:3050`; the managed bridge defaults\nto `http://127.0.0.1:7800`.\n\nPort `3050` is also the existing public-tunnel origin contract. Replacing the\nweb framework or static-interface implementation does not authorize changing\nthat deployed port or the configured public hostname. During a cutover, start\nthe replacement runner on the existing origin first and verify the public\nhealth endpoint before changing any tunnel route.\n\nSupported runner options:\n\n```text\n--host <address>\n--port <0-65535>\n--bridge-url <url>\n--static-dir <directory>\n--no-static\n```\n\nThe equivalent environment settings are:\n\n```text\nOMNIHARNESS_RUNNER_HOST\nOMNIHARNESS_RUNNER_PORT (PORT is a compatibility fallback)\nOMNIHARNESS_BRIDGE_URL\nOMNIHARNESS_STATIC_DIR\nOMNIHARNESS_NO_STATIC=1\nOMNIHARNESS_MANAGE_BRIDGE=0\n```\n\nWith the default build, the runner serves `dist/interface`. `--no-static` is a\nsupported API-only mode. If the default artifact is absent, startup continues\nand emits `runner.static_ui_missing`; if an explicitly supplied `--static-dir`\nis missing or invalid, startup fails. Never combine `--no-static` and\n`--static-dir`.\n\n## Instances, data, and locks\n\n`OMNIHARNESS_ROOT` selects the base data root. `OMNIHARNESS_INSTANCE=name`\nplaces one isolated deployment under\n`$OMNIHARNESS_ROOT/instances/name`. Each instance owns:\n\n```text\nsqlite.db\n.omniharness-auth.key\nrunner.lock.json\nbridge.lock.json\napp-data/run-data/\n```\n\nThe SQLite database and worker JSONL files are one consistency domain. Do not\npoint two live runners at the same instance root. A second process refuses an\nowned runner lock. Separate instances need separate API ports and bridge URLs.\n\n## TLS and reverse proxies\n\nThe Node runner currently terminates HTTP. For any non-loopback deployment,\nterminate HTTPS at a reverse proxy or private tunnel and expose only the API/UI\nport. Keep the ACP bridge on loopback.\n\nForwarding headers are ignored unless the socket peer matches an explicit\ncomma-separated `OMNIHARNESS_TRUSTED_PROXIES` rule. Rules may be exact IPs or\nIPv4 CIDRs:\n\n```text\nOMNIHARNESS_TRUSTED_PROXIES=127.0.0.1,10.20.0.0/16\nOMNIHARNESS_PUBLIC_ORIGIN=https://runner.example.net\n```\n\nConfigure the proxy to replace, not append untrusted client values for,\n`Forwarded`/`X-Forwarded-*`. Never use a catch-all trusted-proxy range.\n\n## Backup and restore\n\nStop the runner before a filesystem backup. Copy the entire instance directory,\nincluding the database, auth key, worker streams, locks, settings, and managed\nmetadata. Exclude only transient build caches. Also back up the deployment's\npassword-hash configuration separately.\n\nRestore into an empty instance path while the runner is stopped, preserve file\npermissions, then start it with the same `OMNIHARNESS_ROOT` and\n`OMNIHARNESS_INSTANCE`. The auth key is required to read encrypted settings and\nvalidate existing sessions. If it is intentionally omitted, rotate the\npassword and expect every client to authenticate again.\n\nClient profile lists and platform-secure bearer sessions are client state, not\npart of a runner backup.\n\n## Disposable smoke check\n\nThis uses an isolated root and a hidden prompt. The password is not passed as a\ncommand-line argument or printed:\n\n```bash\nsmoke_root=\"$(mktemp -d \"${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/omniharness-smoke.XXXXXX\")\"\ntrap 'test -n \"$smoke_root\" && rm -rf -- \"$smoke_root\"' EXIT\nread -r -s -p \"Temporary runner password: \" smoke_password\nprintf '\\n'\nexport OMNIHARNESS_AUTH_PASSWORD=\"$smoke_password\"\nunset smoke_password\nOMNIHARNESS_ROOT=\"$smoke_root\" \\\nOMNIHARNESS_INSTANCE=smoke \\\npnpm runner --host 127.0.0.1 --port 3059 --no-static\n```\n\nIn another terminal, check liveness with:\n\n```bash\ncurl --fail --silent --show-error http://127.0.0.1:3059/api/healthz\n```\n\nPress Ctrl-C in the runner terminal. The trap removes only the temporary root\ncreated by this command.\n\n--- SECURITY DOC ---\n# Authentication, sessions, and TLS\n\n## One password, separate sessions\n\nEach runner has one shared login password. The password is verified only during\nlogin and is never persisted by a client. A successful login creates a\nseparate, listable, revocable session:\n\n- same-origin browser sessions use an HttpOnly cookie;\n- browser/PWA connections to another runner use a same-runner approval window,\n  S256 PKCE, and a bearer session;\n- Electron, Capacitor, VS Code, and CLI hosts submit the password through their\n  trusted host process and keep the returned bearer token outside the\n  renderer/WebView.\n\nBrowser sessions have a 30-day idle and 90-day absolute limit. Native bearer\nsessions have a 90-day idle and 365-day absolute limit. plane, preferably CLI-accessible, for inspection, replay, admin operations, and end-to-end testing without the UI.\n- explicit propagation of real errors to user-facing and operator-facing surfaces and retries,\n- stack traces and failure context,\n- state transitions,\n- timestamps and identifiers needed to reconstruct what happened later.\n\n### Onboarding And Discoverability\n\nAsk what a first-time or returning user sees:\n\n- first-run guidance,\n- empty states,\n- obvious next action,\n- terminology and labels that make sense.\n\n### Risk And Trust Surfaces\n\nAsk where user trust Product\n\nDescribe what the finished product wants to become if fully realized. Be ambitious. \"What controls did the user mention?\" Ask, \"What does the user need to do, recover from, revisit, understand, or change?\" The interface and system behaviors should be inferred from those stories.\n\n## Story Categories To Derive\n\nFor app, UI, and product-surface work, derive stories in these categories when relevant:\n\n- primary journey stories,\n- first-run and empty-state stories,\n- return/revisit stories,\n- failure and recovery stories,\n- status-awareness stories,\n- mutation stories,\n- mobile-use stories.\n\n## What Each Category Means\n\n### Primary Journey Stories\n\nWhat is the main task the user is here to complete?\n\nExamples:\n\n- \"As a user, I want to start a conversation with an agent so I can get work done.\"\n- \"As a user, I want to create a task and move it through a board.\"\n\nThese stories usually imply the core surface, main action affordances, and the path from entry to completion.\n\n### First-Run And Empty-State Stories\n\nWhat happens when nothing exists yet?\n\nExamples:\n\n- \"As a first-time user, I want to understand how to begin.\"\n- \"As a user with no conversations yet, I want an obvious way to start one.\"\n\nThese stories imply onboarding affordances, empty states, and entry-point actions.\n\n### Return/Revisit Stories\n\nHow does a user come back later and continue?\n\nExamples:\n\n- \"As a user, I want to find a previous conversation and continue it.\"\n- \"As a user, I want to reopen a document I edited yesterday.\"\n\nThese stories imply lists, recents, navigation hierarchy, and persistence visibility.\n\n### Failure And Recovery Stories\n\nWhat happens when the happy path fails?\n\nExamples:\n\n- \"As a user, I want to know when a request failed and what I can do next.\"\n- \"As a user, I want to retry after a transient failure without losing my work.\"\n\nThese stories imply error notices, retry flows, recovery actions, and backend/frontend coordination.\n\n### Status-Awareness Stories\n\nWhat does the user need to understand about current state?\n\nExamples:\n\n- \"As a user, I want to know whether the agent is still running, waiting for me, or finished.\"\n- \"As a user, I want to know whether my changes were saved.\"\n\nThese stories imply spinners, badges, state labels, progress indicators, and completion signals.\n\nPersistence questions often cut across these categories. When a story depends on preferences, drafts, history, or configuration, ask what must persist, where it should live, and what the user expects to survive across sessions and devices.\n\n### Mutation Stories\n\nHow does a user revise, retry, fork, resend, undo, or continue from earlier state?\n\nExamples:\n\n- \"As a user, I want to edit an earlier prompt and resend from there.\"\n- \"As a user, I want to fork a conversation from a prior turn.\"\n- \"As a user, I want to retry a failed generation.\"\n\nThese stories imply edit/resend flows, truncation behavior, forking, retry actions, and explicit state transitions.\n\n### Mobile-Use Stories\n\nHow does the same job get done on a smaller screen?\n\nExamples:\n\n- \"As a mobile user, I still need to navigate conversations and act on the current thread.\"\n\nThese stories imply drawers, sheets, responsive prioritization, and compact affordances.\n\n## How To Infer Interface And System Behavior\n\nFor each derived story, ask:\n\n1. What interface affordance does this require?\n2. What system behavior does this require?\n3. What visible state does the user need?\n4. What happens when this fails?\n5. What has to be preserved when the user comes back later?\n6. Which settings or preferences does this touch, and should each persist?\n7. Where should that persisted state live, and who owns it?\n8. What happens on reset, migration, logout, or device change?\n\nAlso ask:\n\n9. What product state does this touch?\n10. What observability or status signal should exist?\n11. What would make this feel untrustworthy if it went wrong?\n\n## What Counts As Obvious Vs Debatable\n\n### Obvious Story-Derived Additions\n\nInclude by default when they are clearly implied by the stories:\n\n- lists or history for return/revisit stories,\n- status indicators for status-awareness stories,\n- error notices and retry paths for failure/recovery stories,\n- empty states for first-run stories,\n- edit/retry/resend actions when mutation stories are core to the product's job.\n\n### Debatable Additions\n\nConfirm with the user before locking them in:\n\n- expensive or complex additions,\n- opinionated product bets,\n- large scope expansions,\n- advanced collaboration, analytics, or automation features,\n- behaviors that are plausible but not clearly implied by the approved stories.\n\n## Role Of Archetype References\n\nUse `v1-product-completeness.md` after the story-derived pass:\n\n- as a sanity check,\n- as a prior for familiar product types,\n- as a way to catch obvious omissions.\n\nDo not use archetype references as a replacement for deriving stories from the actual user request.\n# V1 Product Completeness Reference\n\nUse this reference during brainstorming when the request involves a familiar app or product surface. The goal is not to invent extra features. The goal is to avoid shipping a literal shell that lacks the expected surfaces and states needed for a usable v1.\n\nThis file is a sanity check and prior, not the primary source of truth. Derive completeness from user stories and journeys first. Use this reference afterward to catch obvious omissions for familiar archetypes.\n\n## How To Use This Reference\n\n1. Derive user stories and journeys from the request first.\n2. Identify the closest product archetype.\n3. Expand the design into:\n   - explicitly requested capabilities,\n   - baseline expected v1 surfaces and states.\n4. Keep obvious, conventional additions as baseline expected v1 scope.\n5. Confirm non-obvious, expensive, risky, or strongly opinionated additions with the user before locking them in.\n\n## Questions To Ask For Any Archetype\n\n- What is the primary user journey?\n- What does first-run or empty state look like?\n- What does loading, waiting, or in-progress state look like?\n- What does success or completed state look like?\n- What does failure or recovery look like?\n- How does a user find prior work again later?\n- What navigation and hierarchy are expected?\n- What is different on desktop versus mobile?\n\n## AI Chat / Agent Harness\n\n### Baseline completed, and failed status,\n- input area with obvious send/submit affordance,\n- empty state when no conversation exists,\n- path to resume or revisit prior conversations,\n- mobile-safe navigation pattern such as a drawer or sheet.\n\n### Confirm With User Before Locking In\n\n- advanced filtering or search,\n- rich multi-pane monitoring surfaces,\n- forked conversations,\n- advanced ## Codex final · 2026-08-05T20:33:35.200Z

It is not handoff-ready yet. macOS/Linux will probably install, but the onboarding has several real gaps:

- The README still contains stale Rust/prebuilt-binary instructions.
- Tailscale is not documented; Cloudflare is recommended first.
- Windows lacks the same one-command launcher.
- The production launcher still checks an old `.next` build instead of the current Vite UI.
- The clone command still contains `<repo-url>`.
- `pnpm runner --help` crashes instead of showing usage.

I recommend the complete installer path:

1. `./omniharness` on macOS/Linux and `.\omniharness.ps1` on Windows install dependencies, configure authentication, install published ACP packages, build the UI, and start everything.
2. The API and production UI remain one service on port `3050`; the private ACP bridge remains loopback-only on `7800`.
3. Add `pnpm setup:tailscale` to explicitly configure private HTTPS access using `tailscale serve --bg http://127.0.0.1:3050`.
4. Tailscale becomes the primary README path. Cloudflare becomes an optional public-access alternative.
5. Add clean-machine CI installation checks for macOS, Linux, and Windows, including API health, UI delivery, ACP startup, and GPT‑5.6 Sol metadata.
6. Update the README and deployment/security documentation so they describe the actual installation.

The alternatives are documentation-only—which leaves Windows and installer problems—or Docker-first—which makes local agent authentication and filesystem access more awkward. The approach above is the reliable native setup.

Should I implement that complete path, including the Windows launcher and explicit Tailscale setup command?

Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |\n| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |\n| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |\n\n## Why Order Matters\n\n**\"I'll write tests after to verify it works\"**\n\nTests written after code pass immediately. Passing immediately proves nothing:\n- Might test wrong thing\n- Might test implementation, not behavior\n- Might miss edge cases you forgot\n- You never saw it catch the bug\n\nTest-first forces you to see the test fail, proving it actually tests something.\n\n**\"I already manually tested all the edge cases\"**\n\nManual testing is ad-hoc. You think you tested everything but:\n- No record of what you tested\n- Can't re-run when code changes\n- Easy to forget cases under pressure\n- \"It worked when I tried it\" ≠ comprehensive\n\nAutomated tests are systematic. They run the same way every time.\n\n**\"Deleting X hours of work is wasteful\"**\n\nSunk cost fallacy. The time is already gone. Your choice now:\n- Delete and rewrite with TDD (X more hours, high confidence)\n- Keep it and add tests after (30 min, low confidence, likely bugs)\n\nThe \"waste\" is keeping code you can't trust. Working code without real tests is technical debt.\n\n**\"TDD is dogmatic, being pragmatic means adapting\"**\n\nTDD IS pragmatic:\n- Finds bugs before commit (faster than debugging after)\n- Prevents regressions (tests catch breaks immediately)\n- Documents behavior (tests show how to use code)\n- Enables refactoring (change freely, tests catch breaks)\n\n\"Pragmatic\" shortcuts = debugging in production = slower.\n\n**\"Tests after achieve the same goals - it's spirit not ritual\"**\n\nNo. Tests-after answer \"What does this do?\" Tests-first answer \"What should this do?\"\n\nTests-after are biased by your implementation. You test what you built, not what's required. You verify remembered edge cases, not discovered ones.\n\nTests-first force edge case discovery before implementing. Tests-after verify you remembered everything (you didn't).\n\n30 minutes of tests after ≠ TDD. You get coverage, lose proof tests work.\n\n## Common Rationalizations\n\n| Excuse | Reality |\n|--------|---------|\n| \"Too simple to test\" | Simple code breaks. No record, can't re-run. |\n| \"Deleting X hours is wasteful\" | Sunk cost fallacy. Keeping unverified code is technical debt. |\n| \"Keep as reference, write tests first\" | You'll adapt it.
