Start over with TDD.**\n\n## Example: Bug Fix\n\n**Bug:** Empty email accepted\n\n**RED**\n```typescript\ntest('rejects empty email', async () => {\n  const result = await submitForm({ email: '' });\n  expect(result.error).toBe('Email required');\n});\n```\n\n**Verify RED**\n```bash\n$ npm test\nFAIL: expected 'Email required', got undefined\n```\n\n**GREEN**\n```typescript\nfunction submitForm(data: FormData) {\n  if (!data.email?.trim()) {\n    return { error: 'Email required' };\n  }\n  // ...\n}\n```\n\n**Verify GREEN**\n```bash\n$ npm test\nPASS\n```\n\n**REFACTOR**\nExtract validation for multiple fields if needed.\n\n## Verification Checklist\n\nBefore marking work complete:\n\n- [ ] Every new function/method has a test\n- [ ] Watched each test fail before implementing\n- [ ] Each test failed for expected reason (feature missing, not typo)\n- [ ] Wrote minimal code to pass each test\n- [ ] All tests pass\n- [ ] Output pristine (no errors, warnings)\n- [ ] Tests use real code (mocks only if unavoidable)\n- [ ] The delivered functionality is real, not a fake component, placeholder, canned response, or fallback pretending to work\n- [ ] Edge cases and errors covered\n\nCan't check all boxes? You skipped TDD. Start over.\n\n## When Stuck\n\n| Problem | Solution |\n|---------|----------|\n| Don't know how to test | Write wished-for API. Write assertion first. Ask your human partner. |\n| Test too complicated | Design too complicated. Simplify interface. |\n| Must mock everything | Code too coupled. Use dependency injection. |\n| Test setup huge | Extract helpers. Still complex? Simplify design. |\n\n## Debugging Integration\n\nBug found? Write failing test reproducing it. Follow TDD cycle. Test proves fix and prevents regression.\n\nNever fix bugs without a test.\n\n## Testing Anti-Patterns\n\nWhen adding mocks or test utilities, read @testing-anti-patterns.md to avoid common pitfalls:\n- Testing mock behavior instead of real behavior\n- Adding test-only methods to production classes\n- Mocking without understanding dependencies\n\n## Final Rule\n\n```\nProduction code → test exists and failed first\nOtherwise → not TDD\n```\n\nNo exceptions without your human partner's permission.\n---\nname: systematic-debugging\ndescription: Use when encountering any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior, before proposing fixes\n---\n\n# Systematic Debugging\n\n## Overview\n\nRandom fixes waste time and create new bugs. Quick patches mask underlying issues.\n\n**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.\n\n**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**\n\n## The Iron Law\n\n```\nNO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST\n```\n\nIf you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.\n\n## When to Use\n\nUse for ANY technical issue:\n- Test failures\n- Bugs in production\n- Unexpected behavior\n- Performance problems\n- Build failures\n- Integration issues\n\n**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**\n- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)\n- \"Just one quick fix\" seems obvious\n- You've already tried multiple fixes\n- Previous fix didn't work\n- You don't fully understand the issue\n\n**Don't skip when:**\n- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)\n- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)\n- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)\n\n## The Four Phases\n\nYou MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.\n\n### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation\n\n**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**\n\n1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**\n   - Don't skip past errors or warnings\n   - They often contain the exact solution\n   - Read stack traces completely\n   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes\n\n2. **Reproduce Consistently**\n   - Can you trigger it reliably?\n   - What are the exact steps?\n   - Does it happen every time?\n   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess\n\n3. **Check Recent Changes**\n   - What changed that could cause this?\n   - Git diff, recent commits\n   - New dependencies, config changes\n   - Environmental differences\n\n4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**\n\n   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**\n\n   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**\n   ```\n   For EACH component boundary:\n     - Log what data enters component\n     - Log what data exits component\n     - Verify environment/config propagation\n     - Check state at each layer\n\n   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks\n   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component\n   THEN investigate that specific component\n   ```\n\n   **Example (multi-layer system):**\n   ```bash\n   # Layer 1: Workflow\n   echo \"=== Secrets available in workflow: ===\"\n   echo \"IDENTITY: ${IDENTITY:+SET}${IDENTITY:-UNSET}\"\n\n   # Layer 2: Build script\n   echo \"=== Env vars in build script: ===\"\n   env | grep IDENTITY || echo \"IDENTITY not in environment\"\n\n   # Layer 3: Signing script\n   echo \"=== Keychain state: ===\"\n   security list-keychains\n   security find-identity -v\n\n   # Layer 4: Actual signing\n   codesign --sign \"$IDENTITY\" --verbose=4 \"$APP\"\n   ```\n\n   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)\n\n5. **Trace Data Flow**\n\n   **WHEN error is deep in call stack:**\n\n   See `root-cause-tracing.md` in this directory for the complete backward tracing technique.\n\n   **Quick version:**\n   - Where does bad value originate?\n   - What called this with bad value?\n   - Keep tracing up until you find the source\n   - Fix at source, not at symptom\n\n### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis\n\n**Find the pattern before fixing:**\n\n1. **Find Working Examples**\n   - Locate similar working code in same codebase\n   - What works that's similar to what's broken?\n\n2. **Compare Against References**\n   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY\n   - Don't skim - read every line\n   - Understand the pattern fully before applying\n\n3. **Identify Differences**\n   - What's different between working and broken?\n   - List every difference, however small\n   - Don't assume \"that can't matter\"\n\n4. **Understand Dependencies**\n   - What other components does this need?\n   - What settings, config, environment?\n   - What assumptions does it make?\n\n### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing\n\n**Scientific method:**\n\n1. **Form Single Hypothesis**\n   - State clearly: \"I think X is the root cause because Y\"\n   - Write it down\n   - Be specific, not vague\n\n2. **Test Minimally**\n   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis\n   - One variable at a time\n   - Don't fix multiple things at once\n\n3. **Verify Before Continuing**\n   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4\n   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis\n   - DON'T add more fixes on top\n\n4. **When You Don't Know**\n   - Say \"I don't understand X\"\n   - Don't pretend to know\n   - Ask for help\n   - Research more\n\n### Phase 4: Implementation\n\n**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**\n\n1. **Create Failing Test Case**\n   - Simplest possible reproduction\n   - Automated test if possible\n   - One-off test script if no framework\n   - MUST have before fixing\n   - Use the `ultrapowers:test-driven-development` skill for writing proper failing tests\n\n2. **Implement Single Fix**\n   - Address the root cause identified\n   - ONE change at a time\n   - No \"while I'm here\" improvements\n   - No bundled refactoring\n\n3. **Verify Fix**\n   - Test passes now?\n   - No other tests broken?\n   - Issue actually resolved?\n   - If the bug was meaningful or systemic, use `ultrapowers:learning-from-bugs` before declaring the fix complete.\n\n4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**\n   - STOP\n   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?\n   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information\n   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**\n   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion\n\n5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**\n\n   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**\n   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place\n   - Fixes require \"massive refactoring\" to implement\n   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere\n\n   **STOP and question fundamentals:**\n   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?\n   - Are we \"sticking with it through sheer inertia\"?\n   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?\n\n   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**\n\n   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.\n\n## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process\n\nIf you catch yourself thinking:\n- \"Quick fix for now, investigate later\"\n- \"Just try changing X and see if it works\"\n- \"Add multiple changes, run tests\"\n- \"Skip the test, I'll manually verify\"\n- \"It's probably X, let me fix that\"\n- \"I don't fully understand but this might work\"\n- \"Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently\"\n- \"Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]\"\n- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow\n- **\"One more fix attempt\" (when already tried 2+)**\n- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**\n\n**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**\n\n**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)\n\n## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong\n\n**Watch for these redirections:**\n- \"Is that not happening?\" - You assumed without verifying\n- \"Will it show us...?\" - You should have added evidence gathering\n- \"Stop guessing\" - You're proposing fixes without understanding\n- \"Ultrathink this\" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms\n- \"We're stuck?\" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working\n\n**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.\n\n## Common Rationalizations\n\n| Excuse | Reality |\n|--------|---------|\n| \"Issue is simple, don't need process\" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |\n| \"Emergency, no time for process\" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |\n| \"Just try this first, then investigate\" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |\n| \"I'll write test after confirming fix works\" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |\n| \"Multiple fixes at once saves time\" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |\n| \"Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern\" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |\n| \"I see the problem, let me fix it\" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |\n| \"One more fix attempt\" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |\n\n## Quick Reference\n\n| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |\n|-------|---------------|------------------|\n| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |\n| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |\n| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |\n| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |\n\n## When Process Reveals \"No Root Cause\"\n\nIf systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:\n\n1. You've completed the process\n2. Document what you investigated\n3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)\n4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation\n\n**But:** 95% of \"no root cause\" cases are incomplete investigation.\n\n## Supporting Techniques\n\nThese techniques are part of systematic debugging and available in this directory:\n\n- **`root-cause-tracing.md`** - Trace bugs backward through call stack to find original trigger\n- **`defense-in-depth.md`** - Add validation at multiple layers after finding root cause\n- **`condition-based-waiting.md`** - Replace arbitrary timeouts with condition polling\n\n**Related skills:**\n- **ultrapowers:test-driven-development** - For creating failing test case (Phase 4, Step 1)\n- **ultrapowers:learning-from-bugs** - Record reusable lessons from meaningful architecture, storage, memory, persistence, control-plane, and system-level bugs\n- **ultrapowers:verification-before-completion** - Verify fix worked before claiming success\n\n## Real-World Impact\n\nFrom debugging sessions:\n- Systematic approach: 15-30 minutes to fix\n- Random fixes approach: 2-3 hours of thrashing\n- First-time fix rate: 95% vs 40%\n- New bugs introduced: Near zero vs common\n"

\"\";\n  if (!instance) {\n    return null;\n  }\n  if (!/^[a-zA-Z0-9][a-zA-Z0-9._-]{0,63}$/.test(instance)) {\n    throw new TypeError(\n      \"OMNIHARNESS_INSTANCE must contain only letters, digits, dots, underscores, or dashes.\",\n    );\n  }\n  return instance;\n}\n\nexport function resolveRunnerConfig({\n  argv,\n  cwd,\n  env,\n}: ResolveRunnerConfigOptions): RunnerConfig {\n  const { values: args, flags } = readArgs(argv);\n  const repositoryRoot = path.resolve(cwd);\n  const configuredRoot = env.OMNIHARNESS_ROOT?.trim();\n  const baseRoot = path.resolve(configuredRoot || repositoryRoot);\n  const instance = normalizeInstanceName(env.OMNIHARNESS_INSTANCE);\n  const instanceRoot = instance\n    ? path.join(baseRoot, \"instances\", instance)\n    : baseRoot;\n  const bridgeUrl = args.get(\"--bridge-url\")\n    ?? env.OMNIHARNESS_BRIDGE_URL?.trim()\n    ?? \"http://127.0.0.1:7800\";\n  try {\n    new URL(bridgeUrl);\n  } catch {\n    throw new TypeError(\"--bridge-url must be a valid URL.\");\n  }\n\n  const explicitStaticDir = args.get(\"--static-dir\")\n    ?? env.OMNIHARNESS_STATIC_DIR?.trim()\n    ?? null;\n  const staticDisabled = flags.has(\"--no-static\")\n    || [\"1\", \"true\"].includes(env.OMNIHARNESS_NO_STATIC?.trim().toLowerCase() ?? \"\");\n  if (staticDisabled && explicitStaticDir) {\n    throw new TypeError(\"--no-static cannot be combined with --static-dir.\");\n  }\n\n  const interfaceDevUrl = args.get(\"--interface-dev-url\")\n    ?? env.OMNIHARNESS_INTERFACE_DEV_URL?.trim()\n    ?? null;\n  if (interfaceDevUrl) {\n    let parsed: URL;\n    try {\n      parsed = new URL(interfaceDevUrl);\n    } catch {\n      throw new TypeError(\"--interface-dev-url must be a valid URL.\");\n    }\n    if (parsed.protocol !== \"http:\") {\n      throw new TypeError(\"--interface-dev-url must use http.\");\n    }\n  }\n  return {\n    host: args.get(\"--host\")\n      ?? env.OMNIHARNESS_RUNNER_HOST?.trim()\n      ?? \"0.0.0.0\",\n    port: readPort(\n      args.get(\"--port\")\n        ?? env.OMNIHARNESS_RUNNER_PORT\n        ?? env.PORT,\n      \"--port\",\n      3050,\n    ),\n    bridgeUrl,\n    manageBridge: ![\"0\", \"false\"].includes(\n      env.OMNIHARNESS_MANAGE_BRIDGE?.trim().toLowerCase() ?? \"\",\n    ),\n    repositoryRoot,\n    instanceRoot,\n    databasePath: path.join(instanceRoot, \"sqlite.db\"),\n    bridgeLockPath: path.join(instanceRoot, \"bridge.lock.json\"),\n    runnerLockPath: path.join(instanceRoot, \"runner.lock.json\"),\n    staticDir: staticDisabled\n      ? null\n      : explicitStaticDir\n        ? path.resolve(explicitStaticDir)\n        : path.join(repositoryRoot, \"dist\", \"interface\"),\n    staticDirExplicit: explicitStaticDir !== null,\n    staticDisabled,\n    interfaceDevUrl,\n  };\n}\npackage.json:2:  \"name\": \"omniharness\",\npackage.json:9:    \"omniharness\": \"./omniharness\"\nscripts/ensure-recommended-tools.sh:5:  echo \"[omniharness] Skipping recommended tool setup.\"\nscripts/ensure-recommended-tools.sh:10:  echo \"[omniharness] ripgrep detected.\"\nscripts/ensure-recommended-tools.sh:68:echo \"[omniharness] ripgrep (rg) is recommended for agent repository search.\"\nscripts/ensure-recommended-tools.sh:69:echo \"[omniharness] Attempting to install ripgrep with the system package manager...\"\nscripts/ensure-recommended-tools.sh:72:  echo \"[omniharness] ripgrep installed.\"\nscripts/ensure-recommended-tools.sh:76:echo \"[omniharness] Could not install ripgrep automatically. \"opencode: not detected\"\n   725\tfi\n   726\t\n   727\techo \"\"\n   728\techo \"Checking agent tool environment...\"\n   729\techo \"The OmniHarness agent runtime builds a managed worker PATH from shims: apply_patch, applypatch, codex-linux-sandbox.\"\n   734\telse\n   735\t  echo \"Codex workers also get native Codex argv0 shims: apply_patch, applypatch.\"\n   736\tfi\n   737\techo \"Codex core tools are enabled through a runtime managed config: exec_command, write_stdin, update_plan, apply_patch, web_search, view_image, MCP resources.\"\n   738\tfor tool in rg git node bash sh ls; do\n   739\t  report_tool \"$tool\" \"required\"\n   740\tdone\n   741\tfor tool in pnpm npm python3 python zsh sed awk grep find xargs mkdir rm cp mv jq gh cargo uv fd make; do\n   742\t  report_tool \"$tool\" \"optional\"\n   743\tdone\n   744\t\n   745\techo \"Done.\"\n   260\tThen run the installer directly when you are ready:\n   261\t\n   262\t```bash\n   263\tscripts/install-agent-acp.sh\n   264\t```\n   265\t\n   266\tThe setup script detects supported local coding agents and installs or refreshes\n   267\tthe ACP adapters they need. Codex uses a prebuilt `codex-acp` binary by default\n   268\tfor macOS/Linux on arm64/x64 and Windows x64. Claude's adapter is installed from npm, while\n   269\tGemini and OpenCode expose native ACP commands and do not need separate adapter\n   270\tinstalls. The setup script also checks common agent tools including `rg`, `git`,\n   271\t`node`, shell/file utilities, package managers, Python, `jq`, `gh`, `cargo`,\n   272\t`uv`, `fd`, and `make`.\n   273\t\n   274\t### Prebuilt Codex ACP\n   275\t\n   276\tOmniHarness avoids compiling `codex-acp` with host Rust by default. In `auto`\n   277\tmode, the installer downloads the matching release asset:\n   278\t\n   279\t```text\n   280\tcodex-acp-darwin-arm64\n   281\tcodex-acp-darwin-x64\n   282\tcodex-acp-linux-arm64\n   283\tcodex-acp-linux-x64\n   284\tcodex-acp-windows-x64.exe\n   285\t```\n   286\t\n   287\tUseful overrides:\n   288\t\n   289\t```bash\n   290\tOMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_INSTALL=binary\n   291\tOMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_RELEASE_REPO=danduma/omniharness\n   292\tOMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_RELEASE_TAG=codex-acp-latest\n   293\tOMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_DOWNLOAD_BASE_URL=https://github.com/danduma/omniharness/releases/download/codex-acp-latest\n   294\tOMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_INSTALL_DIR=/custom/bin\n   295\t```\n   296\t\n   297\tOn Windows, use the PowerShell installer to download `codex-acp.exe` into\n   298\t`%LOCALAPPDATA%\\OmniHarness\\bin`:\n   299\t\n   300\t```powershell\n   301\tpowershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\\install-agent-acp.ps1 -AddToPath\n   302\t```\n   303\t\n   304\tGit Bash/MSYS users can also run `scripts/install-agent-acp.sh`; it installs\n   305\tthe Windows release asset as `codex-acp.exe`.\n   306\t\n   307\tFor local development against the Rust source, force Cargo mode:\n   308\t\n   309\t```bash\n   310\tscripts/install-agent-acp.sh --codex-acp=cargo\n   311\t```\n   312\t\n   313\t### Docker-backed Codex ACP\n   314\t\n   315\tIf the prebuilt binary cannot run on a machine, install a Docker-backed wrapper\n   316\tinstead:\n   317\t\n   318\t```bash\n   319\tOMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_INSTALL=docker ./omniharness\n   320\t```\n   321\t\n   322\tOr run the adapter installer directly:\n   323\t\n   324\t```bash\n   325\tscripts/install-agent-acp.sh --codex-acp=docker\n   326\t```\n   327\t\n   328\tThis builds the local image `omniharness/codex-acp:local`, installs a\n   329\t`codex-acp` wrapper into `~/.local/bin`, and runs the ACP adapter inside Docker\n   330\twhile mounting the current project and Codex credential/config paths. The normal\n   331\tOmniHarness worker `PATH` already includes `~/.local/bin`, so no extra PATH\n   332\tsetup is usually needed.\n   333\t\n   334\tUseful overrides:\n   335\t\n   336\t```bash\n   337\tOMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_DOCKER_IMAGE=ghcr.io/your-org/codex-acp:latest\n   338\tOMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_INSTALL_DIR=/custom/bin\n   339\tOMNIHARNESS_DOCKER_BIN=podman\n   340\tOMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_DOCKER_AS_ROOT=1\n   341\t```\n   342\t\n   343\tOn Podman machines, start the VM first if needed:\n   344\t\n   345\t```bash\n   346\tpodman machine start\n   347\tOMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_INSTALL=docker OMNIHARNESS_DOCKER_BIN=podman ./omniharness\n   348\t```\n   349\t\n   350\tIf you build the image locally instead of using a prebuilt image, give the\n   351\tPodman VM more than the default 2 GiB memory:\n   352\t\n   353\t```bash\n   354\tpodman machine stop\n   355\tpodman machine set --memory 8192\n   356\tpodman machine start\n   357\t```\n   358\t\n   359\tThe container includes Node.js, Codex CLI, `codex-acp`, `git`, `rg`, Python,\n   360\t`jq`, `make`, and common shell tools. Project commands run inside the Linux\n   361\tcontainer, so host-only tools still need to be installed in the image or run via\n   362\ta non-Docker adapter.\n   363\t\n   364\t## Development\n   365\t\n   366\tRun the runner and Vite interface together:\n   367\t\n   368\t```bash\n   369\tpnpm dev\n   370\t```\n   371\t\n   372\tOr run them independently:\n   373\t\n   374\t```bash\n   375\tpnpm runner --host 127.0.0.1 --port 3050\n   376\tpnpm dev:interface\n   377\t```\n   378\t\n   379\tRun checks before opening a pull request:\n   380\t\n   381\t```bash\n   382\tpnpm test\n   383\tpnpm build\n   384\t```\n   385\t\n   386\t## CLI\n   387\t\n   388\tRun the same ACP-backed conversation modes from the terminal:\n   389\t\n   390\t```bash\n   391\t./omni -i -w codex \"implement docs/superpowers/plans/example.md\"\n   392\t./omni -p -w gemini \"write a plan for the CLI parity work\"\n   393\t./omni -w codex \"inspect the current repo state\"\n   394\t```\n   395\t\n   396\tBy default, the CLI starts direct-control conversations, watches the created run, and prints messages, execution events, and worker output updates. Use `-i` for implementation, `-p` for planning, `-w` to choose a worker, `--no-watch` for fire-and-return behavior, or `--json` to print the created conversation payload. The legacy implementation shorthand still works:\n   397\t\n   398\t```bash\n   399\t./omni docs/superpowers/plans/example.md\n   400\t```\n   401\t\n   402\tRun OmniHarness itself as an ACP agent over stdio:\n   403\t\n   404\t```bash\n   405\t./omni acp\n   406\t```\n   407\t\n   408\tIn ACP mode, clients can create sessions, list persisted Omni runs, load or resume a run, fork a fresh ACP session from an existing run, switch between `implementation`, `planning`, and `direct`, prompt OmniHarness to start or continue conversations, and receive streamed run updates as ACP `session/update` notifications.\n   409\t\n   410\t## Runtime Data\n   411\t\n   412\tOmniHarness stores persisted conversation state in SQLite at `sqlite.db` under the app root. The app root is `OMNIHARNESS_ROOT` when set, otherwise the current working directory used to start the app.\n   413\t\n   414\tFor normal local development, inspect runs, messages, workers, execution events, settings, and auth records with:\n   415\t\n   416\t```bash\n   417\tsqlite3 sqlite.db\n   418\t```\n   419\t\n   420\t`.omniharness/` is used for runtime side files such as the managed runtime lock, but it is not the default conversation database location.\n   421\t\n   422\tTo delete all conversations and associated persisted artifacts:\n   423\t\n   424\t```bash\n   425\tscripts/delete-conversations.sh\n   426\t```\n   427\t\n   428\t## Agent Tool Environment\n   429\t\n   430\tACP workers may be launched from a GUI app, service manager, editor integration, or another non-login process. Those environments often do not inherit the same `PATH` as your normal terminal.\n   431\t\n   432\tBefore spawning agents, the OmniHarness runtime builds a managed worker `PATH` that includes:\n   433\t\n   434\t- project `node_modules/.bin`\n   435\t- common user bins such as `~/.cargo/bin`, `~/.local/bin`, `~/.bun/bin`, `~/.opencode/bin`, and pyenv shims\n   436\t- Homebrew, MacPorts, and system bins\n   437\t- the inherited environment `PATH`\n   438\t- login-shell `PATH` when available\n   439\t\n   440\tThis keeps agents from losing essential tools just because the runtime was started from a thin environment. Installing tools globally is still recommended, but the runtime no longer depends only on the parent process `PATH`.\n   441\t\n   442\tInspect runtime-side agent health with:\n   443\t\n   444\t```bash\n   445\tcurl http://127.0.0.1:7800/doctor\n   446\t```\n   447\t\n   448\tThe doctor response reports adapter availability, API key status, endpoint reachability, and tool diagnostics.\n   449\t\n   450\t## External Credential Profiles\n   451\t\n   452\tOmniHarness can apply a generic credential env overlay before spawning any ACP worker. Configure it in Settings -> Agents, set `OMNIHARNESS_CREDENTIAL_PROFILES_DIR` to a directory of profiles, or use the default `.omniharness/credential-profiles` under the OmniHarness root.\n   453\t\n   454\tProfiles are auto-discovered by worker type, so `.omniharness/credential-profiles/claude` applies to Claude workers. You can also set `OMNIHARNESS_CREDENTIAL_PROFILE_CLAUDE=runner` or pass `credentialProfile` to the runtime API.\n   455\t\n   456\tFile-backed profile:\n   457\t\n   458\t```text\n   459\t.omniharness/credential-profiles/claude/\n   460\t  env/\n   461\t    ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL\n   462\t    ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN\n   463\t  unset\n   464\t  expires_at\n   465\t```\n   466\t\n   467\t`unset` is one environment variable per line. `expires_at` is optional and only used for status metadata. Secret values are applied to the child process but only key names are exposed in runtime status.\n   468\t\n   469\tCommand-backed profile:\n   470\t\n   471\t```json\n   472\t{\n   473\t  \"command\": \"/Users/you/.local/bin/baton\",\n   474\t  \"args\": [\"credential-profile\"],\n   475\t  \"timeoutMs\": 5000\n   476\t}\n   477\t```\n   478\t\n   479\tSettings can also point a worker directly at a provider command without a profile folder. For Claude and Baton, set:\n   480\t\n   481\t```text\n   482\tOMNIHARNESS_CREDENTIAL_COMMAND_CLAUDE=/Users/you/.local/bin/baton\n   483\tOMNIHARNESS_CREDENTIAL_COMMAND_ARGS_CLAUDE=[\"credential-profile\"]\n   484\t```\n   485\t\n   486\tThe command must print JSON:\n   487\t\n   488\t```json\n   489\t{\n   490\t  \"env\": { \"ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL\": \"https://api.example\", \"ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN\": \"...\" },\n   491\t  \"unset\": [\"ANTHROPIC_API_KEY\"],\n   492\t  \"expiresAt\": \"2026-06-14T04:23:48.000Z\"\n   493\t}\n   494\t```\n   495\t\n   496\t## Troubleshooting Setup\n   497\t\n   498\t- **`This repository is pnpm-only`:** run commands with `pnpm`, not `npm install` or `yarn`.\n   499\t- **Unsupported pnpm version:** install pnpm 9 or newer, or run `./omniharness` from the repo root so the launcher can use Corepack's known-good default when available.\n   500\t- **Unsupported Node version:** use Node.js 22.13 or newer, but below Node.js 26. If you already installed dependencies with a different Node version, run `pnpm rebuild better-sqlite3 @node-rs/argon2 sharp`.\n   501\t- **Native SQLite binding errors:** run `pnpm rebuild better-sqlite3` under your current supported Node version.\n   502\t- **Windows Corepack `EPERM` under `C:\\Program Files\\nodejs`:** install pnpm into the user npm prefix with the PowerShell commands in Windows Quick Start, then open a new shell or update `$env:Path` for the current one.\n   503\t- **Windows install fails with `'cp' is not recognized` while building `@danduma/i18n`:** update to a checkout that pins `@danduma/i18n` to the Windows-compatible commit in `package.json`, then rerun `pnpm install`.\n   504\t- **`ERR_PNPM_IGNORED_BUILDS` mentions `node-pty`:** current checkouts allow the `node-pty` build in `pnpm-workspace.yaml`. If you are upgrading an older checkout, make sure `allowBuilds.node-pty` is `true`, then rerun `pnpm install`; use `pnpm approve-builds node-pty` only if pnpm still reports the build as pending approval.\n   505\t- **Windows startup fails with `spawn pnpm ENOENT` or `spawn EINVAL`:** update to a checkout that runs pnpm through the Windows command shell from the start scripts. As a temporary workaround, start `pnpm runner` and `pnpm dev:interface` from separate PowerShell windows.\n   506\t- **No supported worker appears:** install or log into at least one supported agent CLI, then run `scripts/install-agent-acp.sh --dry-run` and inspect `curl http://127.0.0.1:7800/doctor`.\n   507\t- **Port already in use:** stop the previous OmniHarness process, or set `PORT` and `OMNIHARNESS_AGENT_RUNTIME_PORT` before starting.\n   508\t- **`http://HOST:3050` times out from another machine:** confirm OmniHarness is listening on `0.0.0.0`, then allow inbound TCP traffic to that port in Windows Firewall and any hosting-provider firewall. Local `http://localhost:3050` can work even when external access is blocked.\n   509\t- **Phone pairing asks for auth:** set `OMNIHARNESS_AUTH_PASSWORD` or `OMNIHARNESS_AUTH_PASSWORD_HASH` in `.env` and restart.\n   510\t\n   511\t## Repository Layout\n   512\t\n   513\t- `src/server` and `src/runtime` - runner, persistence, auth, lifecycle, and HTTP/SSE\n   514\t- `src/interface`, `src/ui`, and `src/components` - shared React interface\n   515\t- `src/runtime-api` - transport-neutral runner API and platform adapters\n   516\t- `src/shared` - pure contracts shared across the runner/interface boundary\n   517\t- `apps/interface`, `apps/electron`, `apps/mobile`, `apps/vscode` - platform hosts\n   518\t- `scripts` - development, setup, runtime, and maintenance scripts\n   519\t- `tests` - Vitest and Playwright coverage\n   520\t- `docs/superpowers` - design notes, specs, and implementation plans used by the project\n   521\t\n   522\t## Contributing\n   523\t\n   524\tIssues and pull requests are welcome. This project is still settling its public contribution process, so keep changes focused and include the checks you ran.\n   525\t\n   526\tGood first contributions include:\n   527\t\n   528\t- setup and installation fixes\n   529\t- clearer docs for supported agents and ACP adapters\n   530\t- focused bug reports with logs from `/doctor`\n   531\t- small UI and CLI ergonomics improvements\n   532\t- tests around conversation recovery, event streaming, and worker lifecycle behavior\n   533\t\n   534\tBefore sending a pull request, run:\n   535\t\n   536\t```bash\n   537\tpnpm test\n   538\tpnpm build\n   539\t```\n   540\t\n   541\t## Security\n   542\t\n   543\tOmniHarness is designed around local-first supervision. The web UI and runtime can start local coding agents that may read and modify files in the projects you point them at. Three unchecked Tailscale preconditions will produce raw, unhelpful failures.**\\n(1) `tailscale serve` needs root/admin on Linux unless `tailscale set --operator=$USER` is set, and elevation on Windows. ## Codex progress · 2026-08-05T20:47:20.509Z

The evidence pass found one more real Mac first-run bug: after the Vite migration, `./omniharness` creates `.env` but `pnpm start` does not load it. That means a freshly generated password can be ignored by the runner. I’m adding that to the failing tests alongside the stale `.next` build check and broken runner help before I change production code.

Expect sharp edges, fast-moving internals, and occasional database or workflow changes. The core local loop is the priority: reliable worker launch, observable agent activity, durable recovery, and straightforward developer setup.\n\n## Requirements\n\n- macOS, Linux, or Windows with a normal developer shell. On Windows, use PowerShell for the setup commands below.\n- Node.js 22.13 or newer, up to but not including Node.js 26. If you use `nvm`, run `nvm use` from the repo root to select the recommended local version.\n- pnpm 9 or newer. The `packageManager` field in `package.json` is a known-good Corepack default, not an exact-version requirement.\n- `ripgrep` (`rg`) is recommended for fast agent repository search. The `./omniharness` launcher installs it automatically when a supported system package manager is available. Set `OMNIHARNESS_SKIP_RECOMMENDED_TOOLS=1` to skip recommended tool setup.\n- At least one supported coding agent when you want to run real workers:\n  - Codex CLI plus `codex-acp`\n  - Claude CLI plus `claude-agent-acp`\n  - Gemini CLI with native ACP mode\n  - OpenCode with native ACP mode\n- Docker, if you want OmniHarness to run `codex-acp` from a container instead\n  of compiling the Rust adapter on the host.\n\n## Quick Start\n\nClone the repo, enter it, and select the recommended Node version:\n\n```bash\ngit clone <repo-url> omniharness\ncd omniharness\nnvm use\n```\n\nStart OmniHarness normally:\n\n```bash\n./omniharness\n```\n\nOn first start, `./omniharness` asks you to create a web login password. Press\nEnter to have it generate one for you. Generated passwords are printed once in\nthe terminal; save that password before continuing. The launcher stores only an\nArgon2 hash in `.env`.\n\nThe launcher opens [http://localhost:3050](http://localhost:3050) when the local\nserver is ready. Set `OMNIHARNESS_OPEN_BROWSER=0` if you do not want it to open a\nbrowser automatically.\n\n`./omniharness` installs dependencies when needed, builds the static interface\nwhen needed, then starts the two processes in one logical runner deployment:\n\n- the API/SSE server and static interface on `http://localhost:3050`\n- the co-located ACP bridge on `http://127.0.0.1:7800`\n\nStart the runner directly with `pnpm runner`. Use `--no-static` for a supported\nAPI-only deployment, or `--static-dir <path>` for an explicit interface\nartifact.\n\n## Clients and deployment\n\nThe browser/PWA is served by any runner with `dist/interface`. The other hosts\nare remote clients and never embed or start a runner:\n\n```bash\npnpm electron:build\npnpm electron:package:local\npnpm vscode:build\npnpm vscode:package\npnpm mobile:sync\n```\n\nOperational and security details:\n\n- [Runner deployment, data roots, proxies, backup, and smoke checks](docs/deployment/runner-operations.md)\n- [Authentication, sessions, credential storage, identity, and TLS](docs/security/authentication-and-tls.md)\n- [Desktop/editor migration, mobile/PWA limits, and v1 non-goals](docs/platforms/client-migration-and-limits.md)\n\n### Windows Quick Start\n\nUse PowerShell from the repo root. If Corepack can write to your Node.js\ninstallation, enable the repo's package manager normally:\n\n```powershell\ncorepack enable\ncorepack prepare pnpm@11.2.2 --activate\n```\n\nIf Corepack fails with an `EPERM` error under `C:\\Program Files\\nodejs`, install\npnpm into the user npm prefix instead:\n\n```powershell\n$prefix = Join-Path $env:APPDATA \"npm\"\nNew-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $prefix | Out-Null\nnpm config set prefix $prefix\n$env:Path = \"$prefix;$env:Path\"\n[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable(\"Path\", \"$prefix;$([Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable(\"Path\", \"User\"))\", \"User\")\nnpm install -g pnpm@11.2.2\n```\n\nThen clone, install, build, and start:\n\n```powershell\ngit clone <repo-url> omniharness\ncd omniharness\npnpm install\nCopy-Item .env.example .env\n# Set OMNIHARNESS_AUTH_PASSWORD or OMNIHARNESS_AUTH_PASSWORD_HASH in .env.\npnpm build\n$env:OMNIHARNESS_OPEN_BROWSER = \"0\"\npnpm start\n```\n\nThe web UI listens on `http://localhost:3050` and the runtime listens on\n`http://127.0.0.1:7800`. For browser access from another machine, allow inbound\nTCP traffic to the web port in Windows Firewall and in any provider firewall, or\nput OmniHarness behind a tunnel or reverse proxy. Do not expose the runtime port\ndirectly to the public internet.\n\nRun the separate restart control app if you want a small remote escape hatch\nwith its own password-gated interface:\n\n```bash\npnpm restart:control\n```\n\nIt listens on port `3099`. Open `http://localhost:3099` to see status, recent\nlogs, and buttons to start OmniHarness in dev or production mode. If you explicitly want the older\nlogin-session `LaunchAgent` behavior, set\n`OMNIHARNESS_RESTART_LAUNCHD_SCOPE=user` before running the installer.\n\nThe script API creates `.omniharness/remote-restart-token` on first run and\naccepts bearer auth:\n\n```bash\ncurl -X POST \"http://HOST:3099/restart?mode=dev\" \\\n  -H \"Authorization: Bearer $(cat .omniharness/remote-restart-token)\"\n```\n\nUse `mode=prod` to launch `./omniharness` instead of `pnpm run dev`.\n\nFor phone access through Cloudflare Tunnel, expose the restart app as a second\nhostname that points to `http://localhost:3099`, for example:\n\n```yaml\ningress:\n  - hostname: horse-battery-staple.omniharness.dev\n    service: http://localhost:3050\n  - hostname: restart-horse-battery-staple.omniharness.dev\n    service: http://localhost:3099\n  - service: http_status:404\n```\n\n## Optional Setup\n\nCreate a local env file only if you want password auth, phone pairing, public-origin links, or API-key based agent/model access:\n\n```bash\ncp .env.example .env\n```\n\nLocal agent CLIs that are already logged in usually work without API keys. If you want the supervisor model or runtime workers to use provider keys from the environment, fill in the relevant variables in `.env`.\n\n## Password Auth\n\nOmniHarness requires a password before the web UI can create an authenticated session or pair a phone.\n\nFor the simplest local setup, run the launcher and follow the prompt:\n\n```bash\n./omniharness\n```\n\nIf `.env` or the current shell already contains `OMNIHARNESS_AUTH_PASSWORD` or\n`OMNIHARNESS_AUTH_PASSWORD_HASH`, the launcher keeps that existing configuration.\n\nChange or reset the password from the repo root:\n\n```bash\npnpm auth:password set\n```\n\nPass the password as an argument when you need a one-line command:\n\n```bash\npnpm auth:password set \"new-password\"\n```\n\nThe command removes active `OMNIHARNESS_AUTH_PASSWORD` and\n`OMNIHARNESS_AUTH_PASSWORD_HASH` lines from `.env`, then writes one fresh\nArgon2 hash. Restart OmniHarness after changing the password.\n\nCheck or test the configured password:[REDACTED] auth:password status\npnpm auth:password verify \"new-password\"\n```\n\nHash-only passwords cannot be printed back out. If `status` says the password is\nhash-only and you do not know it, run `pnpm auth:password set` to replace it.\n\n## Remote Tunnel\n\nFor phone or remote-browser access, expose only the web UI port through your\ntunnel provider. With Cloudflare Tunnel quick tunnels:\n\n```bash\ncloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:3050\n```\n\nCopy the generated `https://...` URL into `.env` and restart OmniHarness:\n\n```bash\nprintf 'OMNIHARNESS_PUBLIC_ORIGIN=%s\\n' 'https://your-tunnel-url' >> .env\n./omniharness\n```\n\nKeep OmniHarness password auth enabled even when your tunnel provider also has\nits own access controls.\n\nThe launcher does not require a global `omniharness` install. Run the app from\nthe checkout with `./omniharness`, and run CLI conversations from the checkout\nwith `./omni`.\n\nPreview the agent adapter setup only when you want to install or refresh\noptional ACP adapters:\n\n```bash\nscripts/install-agent-acp.sh --dry-run\n```\n\nThen run the installer directly when you are ready:\n\n```bash\nscripts/install-agent-acp.sh\n```\n\nThe setup script detects supported local coding agents and installs or refreshes\nthe ACP adapters they need. Codex uses a prebuilt `codex-acp` binary by default\nfor macOS/Linux on arm64/x64 and Windows x64. Claude's adapter is installed from npm, while\nGemini and OpenCode expose native ACP commands and do not need separate adapter\ninstalls. The setup script also checks common agent tools including `rg`, `git`,\n`node`, shell/file utilities, package managers, Python, `jq`, `gh`, `cargo`,\n`uv`, `fd`, and `make`.\n\n### Prebuilt Codex ACP\n\nOmniHarness avoids compiling `codex-acp` with host Rust by default. In `auto`\nmode, the installer downloads the matching release asset:\n\n```text\ncodex-acp-darwin-arm64\ncodex-acp-darwin-x64\ncodex-acp-linux-arm64\ncodex-acp-linux-x64\ncodex-acp-windows-x64.exe\n```\n\nUseful overrides:\n\n```bash\nOMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_INSTALL=binary\nOMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_RELEASE_REPO=danduma/omniharness\nOMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_RELEASE_TAG=codex-acp-latest\nOMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_DOWNLOAD_BASE_URL=https://github.com/danduma/omniharness/releases/download/codex-acp-latest\nOMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_INSTALL_DIR=/custom/bin\n```\n\nOn Windows, use the PowerShell installer to download `codex-acp.exe` into\n`%LOCALAPPDATA%\\OmniHarness\\bin`:\n\n```powershell\npowershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\\install-agent-acp.ps1 -AddToPath\n```\n\nGit Bash/MSYS users can also run `scripts/install-agent-acp.sh`; it installs\nthe Windows release asset as `codex-acp.exe`.\n\nFor local development against the Rust source, force Cargo mode:\n\n```bash\nscripts/install-agent-acp.sh --codex-acp=cargo\n```\n\n### Docker-backed Codex ACP\n\nIf the prebuilt binary cannot run on a machine, install a Docker-backed wrapper\ninstead:\n\n```bash\nOMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_INSTALL=docker ./omniharness\n```\n\nOr run the adapter installer directly:\n\n```bash\nscripts/install-agent-acp.sh --codex-acp=docker\n```\n\nThis builds the local image `omniharness/codex-acp:local`, installs a\n`codex-acp` wrapper into `~/.local/bin`, and runs the ACP adapter inside Docker\nwhile mounting the current project and Codex credential/config paths. This mode is approval-gated because it can spend significant tokens: propose it when useful, but only run it if the user explicitly approves.\n\n## Common Failures\n\n| Claim | Requires | Not Sufficient |\n|-------|----------|----------------|\n| Tests pass | Test command output: 0 failures | Previous run, \"should pass\" |\n| Linter clean | Linter output: 0 errors | Partial check, extrapolation |\n| Build succeeds | Build command: exit 0 | Linter passing, logs look good |\n| Bug fixed | Test original symptom: passes | Code changed, assumed fixed |\n| Meaningful system bug fixed | Learning note plus verification | Fix committed with no durable lesson |\n| React/server state sync works | Stale-response, merge, event-sequence, and ownership tests relevant to the change | UI looked right once |\n| Regression test works | Red-green cycle verified | Test passes once |\n| Agent completed | VCS diff shows changes | Agent reports \"success\" |\n| Requirements met | Line-by-line checklist | Tests passing |\n| Feature complete | Real end-to-end behavior in the product | Mocked component, canned data, placeholder UI, fallback path |\n\n## Red Flags - STOP\n\n- Using \"should\", \"probably\", \"seems to\"\n- Expressing satisfaction before verification (\"Great!\", \"Perfect!\", \"Done!\", etc.)\n- About to commit/push/PR without verification\n- Trusting agent success reports\n- Accepting \"validated with mocks\" or \"placeholder works\" as completion\n- Relying on partial verification\n- Thinking \"just this once\"\n- Tired and wanting work over\n- **ANY wording implying success without having run verification**\n\n## Rationalization Prevention\n\n| Excuse | Reality |\n|--------|---------|\n| \"Should work now\" | RUN the verification |\n| \"I'm confident\" | Confidence ≠ evidence |\n| \"Just this once\" | No exceptions |\n| \"Linter passed\" | Linter ≠ compiler |\n| \"Agent said success\" | Verify independently |\n| \"I'm tired\" | Exhaustion ≠ excuse |\n| \"Partial check is enough\" | Partial proves nothing |\n| \"Different words so rule doesn't apply\" | Spirit over letter |\n\n## Key Patterns\n\n**Tests:**\n```\n✅ [Run test command] [See: 34/34 pass] \"All tests pass\"\n❌ \"Should pass now\" / \"Looks correct\"\n```\n\n**Regression tests (TDD Red-Green):**\n```\n✅ Write → Run (pass) → Revert fix → Run (MUST FAIL) → Restore → Run (pass)\n❌ \"I've written a regression test\" (without red-green verification)\n```\n\n**Build:**\n```\n✅ [Run build] [See: exit 0] \"Build passes\"\n❌ \"Linter passed\" (linter doesn't check compilation)\n```\n\n**Requirements:**\n```\n✅ Re-read plan → Create checklist → Verify each → Report gaps or completion\n❌ \"Tests pass, phase complete\"\n```\n\n**Agent delegation:**\n```\n✅ Agent reports success → Check VCS diff → Verify changes → Report actual state\n❌ Trust agent report\n```\n\n## Why This Matters\n\nFrom 24 failure memories:\n- your human partner said \"I don't believe you\" - trust broken\n- Undefined functions shipped - would crash\n- Missing requirements shipped - incomplete features\n- Time wasted on false completion → redirect → rework\n- Violates: \"Honesty is a core value. If you lie, you'll be replaced.\"\n\n## When To Apply\n\n**ALWAYS before:**\n- ANY variation of success/completion claims\n- ANY expression of satisfaction\n- ANY positive statement about work state\n- Committing, PR creation, task completion\n- Staging, committing, pushing, or opening a PR when the work could include secrets, local environment files, dependencies, caches, build outputs, logs, temporary files, or generated/intermediate artifacts\n- Moving to next task\n- Delegating to agents\n\nWhen a meaningful bug involved architecture, storage, memory, persistence, control planes, background workers, recovery, data loss, security, or a repeated wrong assumption, use `ultrapowers:learning-from-bugs` before claiming the fix is complete.\n\nWhen a React app has server state, optimistic UI, caches, polling, SSE/WebSocket streams, background jobs, or persisted runtime state, use `ultrapowers:client-server-state-invariants` to decide which race and synchronization tests are required before claiming completion.\n\nBefore any git publish step, verify `.gitignore` exists for the project and that `git status` does not include secrets, credentials, local environment files, `node_modules`, dependency caches, build outputs, coverage output, logs, temporary files, or intermediate/generated artifacts unless the human explicitly asked to version a specific generated artifact.\n\n**Rule applies to:**\n- Exact phrases\n- Paraphrases and synonyms\n- Implications of success\n- ANY communication suggesting completion/correctness\n\n## The Bottom Line\n\n**No shortcuts for verification.**\n\nRun the command. Read the output. THEN claim the result.\n\nThis is non-negotiable.\n---\nname: learning-from-bugs\ndescription: Use when a meaningful bug, regression, architecture flaw, storage issue, memory problem, persistence failure, control-plane failure, or system-level failure has been diagnosed or fixed\n---\n\n# Learning From Bugs\n\nWhen a bug teaches something reusable, capture the lesson before moving on.\n\n## Use This For\n\nUse this after diagnosing or fixing bugs that involve:\n\n- architecture or ownership boundaries,\n- storage, persistence, migrations, caching, or file paths,\n- memory management, leaks, lifecycle, cleanup, or resource pressure,\n- concurrency, queues, retries, resumability, or recovery,\n- control planes, event streams, background workers, or long-running jobs,\n- security, data loss, user trust, or incident-like failures,\n- any bug that took repeated attempts or revealed a wrong mental model.\n\nSkip it for typos, obvious one-line UI mistakes, throwaway test fixture fixes, or purely local churn that will not help future work.\n\n## Required Output\n\nWrite a short learning note to:\n\n`docs/superpowers/learnings/YYYY-MM-DD-<bug-or-lesson-slug>.md`\n\nCreate the directory if needed.\n\nUse this shape:\n\n```markdown\n# [Lesson Title]\n\n**Date:** YYYY-MM-DD\n**Context:** [project, feature, or subsystem]\n**Symptom:** [what failed]\n**Root Cause:** [the real cause, not the symptom]\n**Fix:** [what changed]\n**Verification:** [commands, tests, or checks that proved it]\n**Prevention:** [what future agents should do differently]\n**Skill/Doc Updates:** [nearby skills or docs updated, or why no general update was needed]\n```\n\nKeep it concrete. Future agents should be able to read the note and avoid the same mistake.\n\n## Update The System When The Lesson Generalizes\n\nIf the bug reveals a reusable rule, update the nearest skill or defaults doc in the same change. Examples:\n\n- debugging lesson -> `systematic-debugging`\n- verification gap -> `verification-before-completion`\n- control-plane or eventing lesson -> `instrumenting-control-planes`\n- React lifecycle or routing lesson -> `building-react-apps`\n- planning omission -> `writing-plans` or `brainstorming`\n\nDo not bury a general lesson only in a project note. The learning note records the case; the skill update changes future behavior.\n\n## Completion Gate\n\nBefore saying a meaningful bug is fixed, check:\n\n1. Is this lesson reusable?\n2. Is there a learning note?\n3. Did any skill or defaults doc need an update?\n4. Did verification prove the fix?\n\nIf the answer to 1 is yes, do not skip the note. If the answer to 3 is no, say why in the note.\n---\nname: requesting-code-review\ndescription: Use when completing tasks, implementing major features, or before merging to verify work meets requirements\n---\n\n# Requesting Code Review\n\nDispatch ultrapowers:code-reviewer subagent to catch issues before they cascade. The reviewer gets precisely crafted context for evaluation — never your session's history. This keeps the reviewer focused on the work product, not your thought process, and preserves your own context for continued work.\n\n**Core principle:** Review early, review often.\n\n## When to Request Review\n\n**Mandatory:**\n- After each task in subagent-driven development\n- After completing major feature\n- Before merge to main\n\n**Optional but valuable:**\n- When stuck (fresh perspective)\n- Before refactoring (baseline check)\n- After fixing complex bug\n\n## How to Request\n\n**1. Get git SHAs:**\n```bash\nBASE_SHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD~1)  # or origin/main\nHEAD_SHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD)\n```\n\n**2. Dispatch code-reviewer subagent:**\n\nUse Task tool with ultrapowers:code-reviewer type, fill template at `code-reviewer.md`\n\n**Placeholders:**\n- `{WHAT_WAS_IMPLEMENTED}` - What you just built\n- `{PLAN_OR_REQUIREMENTS}` - What it should do\n- `{BASE_SHA}` - Starting commit\n- `{HEAD_SHA}` - Ending commit\n- `{DESCRIPTION}` - Brief summary\n\n**3. Act on feedback:**\n- Fix Critical issues immediately\n- Fix Important issues before proceeding\n- Note Minor issues for later\n- Push back if reviewer is wrong (with reasoning)\n\n## Example\n\n```\n[Just completed Task 2: Add verification function]\n\nYou: Let me request code review before proceeding.\n\nBASE_SHA=$(git log --oneline | grep \"Task 1\" | head -1 | awk '{print $1}')\nHEAD_SHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD)\n\n[Dispatch ultrapowers:code-reviewer subagent]\n  WHAT_WAS_IMPLEMENTED: Verification and repair functions for conversation index\n  PLAN_OR_REQUIREMENTS: Task 2 from docs/superpowers/plans/deployment-plan.md\n  BASE_SHA: a7981ec\n  HEAD_SHA: 3df7661\n  DESCRIPTION: Added verifyIndex() and repairIndex() with 4 issue types\n\n[Subagent returns]:\n  Strengths: Clean architecture, real tests\n  Issues:\n    Important: Missing progress indicators\n    Minor: Magic number (100) for reporting interval\n  Assessment: Ready to proceed\n\nYou: [Fix progress indicators]\n[Continue to Task 3]\n```\n\n## Integration with Workflows\n\n**Subagent-Driven Development:**\n- Review after EACH task\n- Catch issues before they compound\n- Fix before moving to next task\n\n**Executing Plans:**\n- Review after each batch (3 tasks)\n- Get feedback, apply, continue\n\n**Ad-Hoc Development:**\n- Review before merge\n- Review when stuck\n\n## Red Flags\n\n**Never:**\n- Skip review because \"it's simple\"\n- Ignore Critical issues\n- Proceed with unfixed Important issues\n- Argue with valid technical feedback\n\n**If reviewer wrong:**\n- Push back with technical reasoning\n- Show code/tests that prove it works\n- Request clarification\n\nSee template at: requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md\n"

A user who runs `pnpm setup:tailscale` (which writes into `.env`) or sets the port in `.env` gets a launcher that health-checks, prints, and pairs against `localhost:3050` while the server listens elsewhere — `local_omniharness_status` will report the wrong thing and startup guidance/pairing links will be wrong. The launcher must source the same `.env` (or ask the runner for its resolved port) before computing `WEB_PORT`.\\n\\n**2. `setup-tailscale.mjs` rollback destroys unrelated Serve state**\\nBoth the rename-failure path and `--reset` run `tailscale serve --https=443 off`, which disables the entire HTTPS:443 Serve configuration on the device, not just the listener this script added. Combined with `--force` (which lets `serve --bg` overwrite pre-existing config with no saved copy), a user with an existing Serve setup can lose it permanently. Snapshot `serve status --json` before mutating and restore it via `tailscale serve set`/config import on rollback, and scope `--reset` to the mount this tool created.\\n\\n**3. `inspectServeState` mis-detects existing config (two bugs)**\\n- `tailscale serve status --json` emits `null` when nothing is configured on several versions; `Object.keys(null)` throws a `TypeError`, which the `catch` re-throws (only `SyntaxError` is tolerated). Fresh machines can hard-fail here.\\n- `JSON.stringify(status).includes(target)` is a substring test: target `http://127.0.0.1:3050` matches an unrelated existing proxy to `http://127.0.0.1:30500`, so the guard silently passes and the script overwrites that listener. Compare parsed proxy targets exactly.\\n\\n**4. `--env-file-if-exists` has a Node floor that isn't enforced**\\nIt requires Node ≥ 20.12 / 21.7. `pnpm start` and `pnpm runner` now fail with `bad option` on older supported Node. Confirm `.nvmrc` and the engines range enforce this, and note that `--env-file-if-exists=.env` is CWD-relative, so `pnpm start` from a subdirectory silently loses `.env`.\\n\\n## Important bugs\\n\\n**5. `scripts/interface-build-state.mjs` fingerprints whole directories, including generated/untracked files.** `apps/interface`, `src/lib`, `src/interface` etc. are walked with no ignore list beyond `.DS_Store` — no `node_modules`, `.vite`, `dist`, or editor temp filtering, and `fs.stat` follows symlinks (a symlinked or self-referential directory recurses forever). If the build or dev server writes anything under an `INPUT_PATH` (e.g. `apps/interface/.vite`), every launch rebuilds forever. Restrict inputs to tracked source or add an explicit ignore set, and use `lstat`.\\n\\n**6. Launcher exits instead of building when the state script errors.** Any non-10 exit (missing script, permission error, transient ENOENT during the directory walk, symlink recursion from #5) aborts startup with `exit \\\"$BUILD_STATE_EXIT\\\"`. Failing open by rebuilding is the safer default for a user-facing installer.\\n\\n**7. Lockfile comparison likely forces a reinstall on every launch.** `cmp -s pnpm-lock.yaml node_modules/.pnpm/lock.yaml` assumes pnpm always mirrors the lockfile byte-for-byte. It is not written under `node-linker=hoisted`, and it reflects the lockfile *after* pnpm's own normalization, so a repo whose committed lockfile differs cosmetically reinstalls on every start. Gate on the mismatch only after one install attempt, or compare a hash pnpm actually guarantees.\\n\\n**8. The macOS CI job does not verify the stated release goal.** The claim under review is that a fresh user can install *without compiling ACP adapters*, but the workflow never asserts any adapter is present or that no compiler ran — and the launcher swallows adapter failures (`|| echo ... continuing`). As written, the job would pass with every ACP adapter broken. Add an assertion on `install-agent-acp.sh --ensure-only` output/exit and on the resolved adapter binaries.\\n\\n## Minor (not blocking)\\n\\n- `scripts/runner.ts`: help is only recognized when it is the sole argument, so `--port 3050 --help` falls through to config resolution.\\n- Removing the tunnel guidance leaves no in-CLI warning that the runner still defaults to binding `0.0.0.0` until `setup:tailscale` runs.\\n- Staged `.env.omniharness-tailscale.tmp-<pid>` files are left behind if the process is killed between `stageEnv` and rename (mode 0600, so low severity).\\n\\nVERDICT: FIX\\n\"}"

Claude's adapter is installed from\nREADME.md:262:npm, while Gemini and OpenCode expose native ACP commands and need no separate\nREADME.md:265:### Codex ACP Updates\nREADME.md:267:Normal `./omniharness` startup checks the managed Codex ACP and Codex CLI package\nREADME.md:278:OMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_INSTALL=npm\nREADME.md:279:OMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_NPM_ROOT=/custom/package/root\nREADME.md:280:OMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_INSTALL_DIR=/custom/bin\nREADME.md:290:### Docker-backed Codex ACP\nREADME.md:292:If you deliberately want ACP isolation, install a Docker-backed wrapper instead:\nREADME.md:295:OMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_INSTALL=docker ./omniharness\nREADME.md:305:`codex-acp` wrapper into `~/.local/bin`, and runs the ACP adapter inside Docker\nREADME.md:313:OMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_DOCKER_IMAGE=ghcr.io/your-org/codex-acp:latest\nREADME.md:314:OMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_INSTALL_DIR=/custom/bin\nREADME.md:316:OMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_DOCKER_AS_ROOT=1\nREADME.md:323:OMNIHARNESS_CODEX_ACP_INSTALL=docker OMNIHARNESS_DOCKER_BIN=podman ./omniharness\nREADME.md:351:pnpm runner --host 127.0.0.1 --port 3050\nREADME.md:364:Run the same ACP-backed conversation modes from the terminal:\nREADME.md:378:Run OmniHarness itself as an ACP agent over stdio:\nREADME.md:384:In ACP mode, clients can create sessions, list persisted Omni runs, load or resume a run, fork a fresh ACP session from an existing run, switch between `implementation`, `planning`, and `direct`, prompt OmniHarness to start or continue conversations, and receive streamed run updates as ACP `session/update` notifications.\nREADME.md:406:ACP workers may be launched from a GUI app, service manager, editor integration, or another non-login process. Those environments often do not inherit the same `PATH` as your normal terminal.\nREADME.md:412:- Homebrew, MacPorts, and system bins\nREADME.md:428:OmniHarness can apply a generic credential env overlay before spawning any ACP worker. Configure it in Settings -> Agents, set `OMNIHARNESS_CREDENTIAL_PROFILES_DIR` to a directory of profiles, or use the default `.omniharness/credential-profiles` under the OmniHarness root.\nREADME.md:481:- **The private Tailscale URL times out:** run `tailscale status` and `tailscale serve status`, confirm the client device is in the same tailnet and permitted by its access rules, then restart `./omniharness` after setup.\nREADME.md:486:- `src/server` and `src/runtime` - runner, persistence, auth, lifecycle, and HTTP/SSE\nREADME.md:502:- clearer docs for supported agents and ACP adapters\n# OmniHarness\n\nOmniHarness is a local control plane for supervising ACP-backed coding agents.\nOne logical headless runner owns SQLite, auth, supervision, PTYs, and agent\nprocesses; the shared Vite interface runs in the web/PWA, Electron, iOS,\nAndroid, and VS Code and can stay connected to multiple runners.\n\nUse it when you want one durable place to start coding-agent runs, watch worker output, recover conversations, inspect execution events, and keep local agent processes behind a clear supervisory layer.\n\n## What You Get\n\n- **Multi-agent supervision:** start implementation, planning, and direct-control conversations with supported ACP workers.\n- **Live run visibility:** stream messages, worker output, execution events, and status changes while a run is active.\n- **Durable local history:** persist runs, messages, workers, settings, auth records, and execution events in SQLite.\n- **CLI parity:** launch and watch the same conversation modes from the terminal.\n- **ACP server mode:** expose OmniHarness itself as an ACP agent over stdio for compatible clients.\n- **Managed agent environment:** spawn workers with a practical `PATH` even when the app starts from a GUI, editor, or service manager.\n- **Phone-friendly local UI:** run the web app as a local PWA for supervising work away from the terminal.\n- **Multi-runner clients:** save any number of authenticated runners, keep their\n  event streams live, and switch the visible workspace without reconnecting.\n\n## Project Status\n\nOmniHarness is early open-source software under active development. Expect sharp edges, fast-moving internals, and occasional database or workflow changes. The core local loop is the priority: reliable worker launch, observable agent activity, durable recovery, and straightforward developer setup.\n\n## Requirements\n\n- macOS with `git`, `curl`, and a normal Terminal shell. This is the release-gated installation path. Linux uses the same shell launcher but is not a release gate yet.\n- Node.js 22.13 or newer, up to but not including Node.js 26. The launcher selects the repo version through `nvm` and installs `nvm` when necessary.\n- pnpm 9 or newer. The launcher uses an existing compatible pnpm, Corepack, or npm to install the repo's known-good version.\n- `ripgrep` (`rg`) is recommended for fast agent repository search. The `./omniharness` launcher installs it automatically when a supported system package manager is available. Set `OMNIHARNESS_SKIP_RECOMMENDED_TOOLS=1` to skip recommended tool setup.\n- At least one supported coding agent when you want to run real workers:\n  - Codex; the launcher installs the maintained ACP adapter and Codex CLI as published packages\n  - Claude CLI plus `claude-agent-acp`\n  - Gemini CLI with native ACP mode\n  - OpenCode with native ACP mode\n\n## Quick Start\n\nClone the repo and start it:\n\n```bash\ngit clone https://github.com/danduma/omniharness.git\ncd omniharness\n./omniharness\n```\n\nOn first start, `./omniharness` asks you to create a web login password. Press\nEnter to have it generate one for you. Generated passwords are printed once in\nthe terminal; save that password before continuing. The launcher stores only an\nArgon2 hash in `.env`.\n\nThe launcher opens [http://localhost:3050](http://localhost:3050) when the local\nserver is ready. Set `OMNIHARNESS_OPEN_BROWSER=0` if you do not want it to open a\nbrowser automatically.\n\n`./omniharness` checks Node and pnpm, installs repository dependencies, installs\nor refreshes published ACP packages, and builds the Vite interface when its\ncontent fingerprint changes. It then starts one logical runner deployment:\n\n- the API/SSE server and production web interface together on `http://localhost:3050`\n- the co-located ACP bridge on `http://127.0.0.1:7800`\n\nThere is no separate production UI server to install or expose. The separate\nVite process is only for development.\n\nStart the runner directly with `pnpm runner`. Use `--no-static` for a supported\nAPI-only deployment, or `--static-dir <path>` for an explicit interface\nartifact.\n\n## Clients and deployment\n\nThe browser/PWA is served by any runner with `dist/interface`. The other hosts\nare remote clients and never embed or start a runner:\n\n```bash\npnpm electron:build\npnpm electron:package:local\npnpm vscode:build\npnpm vscode:package\npnpm mobile:sync\n```\n\nOperational and security details:\n\n- [Runner deployment, data roots, proxies, backup, and smoke checks](docs/deployment/runner-operations.md)\n- [Authentication, sessions, credential storage, identity, and TLS](docs/security/authentication-and-tls.md)\n- [Desktop/editor migration, mobile/PWA limits, and v1 non-goals](docs/platforms/client-migration-and-limits.md)\n\nRun the separate restart control app if you want a small remote escape hatch\nwith its own password-gated interface:\n\n```bash\npnpm restart:control\n```\n\nIt listens on port `3099`. Open `http://localhost:3099` to see status, recent\nlogs, and buttons to start OmniHarness in dev or production mode. The web login\nuses `OMNIHARNESS_AUTH_PASSWORD_HASH` or `OMNIHARNESS_AUTH_PASSWORD` when either\nis configured, then falls back to `OMNIHARNESS_REMOTE_RESTART_PASSWORD`, then to\nthe generated token file.\n\nTo keep the restart controller alive across reboots even when macOS does not\nauto-login, install the boot-time daemon:\n\n```bash\n./scripts/install-restarter.sh\n```\n\nIt installs as a `LaunchDaemon` by default. If you explicitly want the older\nlogin-session `LaunchAgent` behavior, set\n`OMNIHARNESS_RESTART_LAUNCHD_SCOPE=user` before running the installer.\n\nThe script API creates `.omniharness/remote-restart-token` on first run and\naccepts bearer auth:\n\n```bash\ncurl -X POST \"http://HOST:3099/restart?mode=dev\" \\\n  -H \"Authorization: Bearer $(cat .omniharness/remote-restart-token)\"\n```\n\nUse `mode=prod` to launch `./omniharness` instead of `pnpm run dev`.\n\nFor public access through Cloudflare Tunnel, expose the restart app as a second\nhostname only if you intentionally want that public-tunnel deployment:\n\n```yaml\ningress:\n  - hostname: horse-battery-staple.omniharness.dev\n    service: http://localhost:3050\n  - hostname: restart-horse-battery-staple.omniharness.dev\n    service: http://localhost:3099\n  - service: http_status:404\n```\n\n## Optional Setup\n\nCreate a local env file only if you want password auth, phone pairing, public-origin links, or API-key based agent/model access:\n\n```bash\ncp .env.example .env\n```\n\nLocal agent CLIs that are already logged in usually work without API keys. If you want the supervisor model or runtime workers to use provider keys from the environment, fill in the relevant variables in `.env`.\n\n## Password Auth\n\nOmniHarness requires a password before the web UI can create an authenticated session or pair a phone.\n\nFor the simplest local setup, run the launcher and follow the prompt:\n\n```bash\n./omniharness\n```\n\nIf `.env` or the current shell already contains `OMNIHARNESS_AUTH_PASSWORD` or\n`OMNIHARNESS_AUTH_PASSWORD_HASH`, the launcher keeps that existing configuration.\n\nChange or reset the password from the repo root:\n\n```bash\npnpm auth:password set\n```\n\nPass the password as an argument when you need a one-line command:\n\n```bash\npnpm auth:password set \"new-password\"\n```\n\nThe command removes active `OMNIHARNESS_AUTH_PASSWORD` and\n`OMNIHARNESS_AUTH_PASSWORD_HASH` lines from `.env`, then writes one fresh\nArgon2 hash. Restart OmniHarness after changing the password.\n\nCheck or test the configured password:[REDACTED] auth:password status\npnpm auth:password verify \"new-password\"\n```\n\nHash-only passwords cannot be printed back out. If `status` says the password is\nhash-only and you do not know it, run `pnpm auth:password set` to replace it.\n\n## Private Access With Tailscale\n\nTailscale Serve is the recommended way to reach OmniHarness from another Mac,\nphone, or tablet. It keeps the service inside your tailnet, applies your\nTailscale access rules, and provides a private HTTPS URL. Install the recommended\nstandalone [Tailscale app for macOS](https://tailscale.com/download/mac), sign in,\nand then run:\n\n```bash\npnpm setup:tailscale\n```\n\nThe command verifies the tailnet connection, refuses to overwrite an existing\nLAN or tunnel configuration, configures:\n\n```bash\ntailscale serve --bg http://127.0.0.1:3050\n```\n\nIt then writes the private `https://...ts.net` origin and loopback bind address\nto the ignored local `.env`. Restart OmniHarness afterward:\n\n```bash\n./omniharness\n```\n\nCheck the real private route with `tailscale serve status`, then open the printed\nURL from another device on the tailnet. Password authentication remains required;\ntailnet membership is an additional security boundary, not a replacement.\n\nUseful safe operations:\n\n```bash\npnpm setup:tailscale -- --dry-run  # inspect without changing Tailscale or .env\npnpm setup:tailscale -- --force    # preserve conflicting values as comments, then replace them\npnpm setup:tailscale -- --reset    # disable OmniHarness HTTPS Serve and remove managed settings\n```\n\nIf Serve reports an operator, administrator, MagicDNS, or HTTPS-certificate\nproblem, follow the exact Tailscale error and retry. The setup command leaves\n`.env` unchanged when Serve fails.\n\n### Optional Public Access With Cloudflare\n\nUse a public tunnel only when tailnet-only access is not sufficient. Expose port\n`3050`, never the ACP bridge on `7800`:\n\n```bash\ncloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:3050\n```\n\nSet `OMNIHARNESS_PUBLIC_ORIGIN` in `.env` to the generated HTTPS URL and restart\nOmniHarness. Keep OmniHarness password authentication enabled even when the\ntunnel provider has separate access controls.\n\nThe launcher does not require a global `omniharness` install. Run the app from\n# Runner deployment and operations\n\n## Process model\n\nOne OmniHarness runner is one logical deployment with two co-located\nprocesses:\n\n- the API server owns SQLite, auth, supervision, PTYs, settings, files, and the\n  HTTP/SSE contract;\n- the ACP bridge owns agent processes and listens on loopback by default.\n\nClients connect only to the API server. Electron, iOS, Android, VS Code, and\nbrowser/PWA clients never connect directly to the bridge.\n\n`pnpm runner` starts the API server and starts or adopts a loopback bridge. The\nAPI remains available in a degraded state while a failed bridge retries. All\nstart, adopt, retry, refusal, failure, and shutdown choices emit named events.\n\n## Build and start\n\nBuild the shared static interface and start a normal runner:\n\n```bash\npnpm install\npnpm build\npnpm runner\n```\n\nThe default API/UI address is `http://0.0.0.0:3050`; the managed bridge defaults\nto `http://127.0.0.1:7800`.\n\nPort `3050` is also the existing public-tunnel origin contract. Replacing the\nweb framework or static-interface implementation does not authorize changing\nthat deployed port or the configured public hostname. During a cutover, start\nthe replacement runner on the existing origin first and verify the public\nhealth endpoint before changing any tunnel route.\n\nSupported runner options:\n\n```text\n--host <address>\n--port <0-65535>\n--bridge-url <url>\n--static-dir <directory>\n--no-static\n```\n\nThe equivalent environment settings are:\n\n```text\nOMNIHARNESS_RUNNER_HOST\nOMNIHARNESS_RUNNER_PORT (PORT is a compatibility fallback)\nOMNIHARNESS_BRIDGE_URL\nOMNIHARNESS_STATIC_DIR\nOMNIHARNESS_NO_STATIC=1\nOMNIHARNESS_MANAGE_BRIDGE=0\n```\n\nWith the default build, the runner serves `dist/interface`. `--no-static` is a\nsupported API-only mode. If the default artifact is absent, startup continues\nand emits `runner.static_ui_missing`; if an explicitly supplied `--static-dir`\nis missing or invalid, startup fails. Never combine `--no-static` and\n`--static-dir`.\n\n## Instances, data, and locks\n\n`OMNIHARNESS_ROOT` selects the base data root. `OMNIHARNESS_INSTANCE=name`\nplaces one isolated deployment under\n`$OMNIHARNESS_ROOT/instances/name`. Each instance owns:\n\n```text\nsqlite.db\n.omniharness-auth.key\nrunner.lock.json\nbridge.lock.json\napp-data/run-data/\n```\n\nThe SQLite database and worker JSONL files are one consistency domain. Do not\npoint two live runners at the same instance root. A second process refuses an\nowned runner lock. Separate instances need separate API ports and bridge URLs.\n\n## Private access with Tailscale\n\nTailscale Serve is the preferred remote-access boundary for a Mac runner. From\nthe repository root, run:\n\n```bash\npnpm setup:tailscale\n```\n\nThe setup command validates the connected tailnet, configures persistent private\nHTTPS proxying to `http://127.0.0.1:3050`, and manages only these ignored `.env`\nsettings:\n\n```text\nOMNIHARNESS_PUBLIC_ORIGIN=https://device.tailnet.ts.net\nOMNIHARNESS_RUNNER_HOST=127.0.0.1\n```\n\nRestart `./omniharness`, check `tailscale serve status`, and open the printed URL\nfrom an allowed tailnet device. Use `pnpm setup:tailscale -- --dry-run` to inspect\nthe operation, `--force` to preserve and replace conflicting origin/host values,\nor `--reset` to disable the owned HTTPS listener and remove its managed settings.\nThe command never enables Funnel and never proxies port `7800`.\n\n## TLS and reverse proxies\n\nThe Node runner currently terminates HTTP. For any non-loopback deployment,\nterminate HTTPS at a reverse proxy or private tunnel and expose only the API/UI\nport. Keep the ACP bridge on loopback.\n\nForwarding headers are ignored unless the socket peer matches an explicit\ncomma-separated `OMNIHARNESS_TRUSTED_PROXIES` rule. Rules may be exact IPs or\nIPv4 CIDRs:\n\n```text\nOMNIHARNESS_TRUSTED_PROXIES=127.0.0.1,10.20.0.0/16\nOMNIHARNESS_PUBLIC_ORIGIN=https://runner.example.net\n```\n\nConfigure the proxy to replace, not append untrusted client values for,\n`Forwarded`/`X-Forwarded-*`. Never use a catch-all trusted-proxy range.\n\n## Backup and restore\n\nStop the runner before a filesystem backup. Copy the entire instance directory,\nincluding the database, auth key, worker streams, locks, settings, and managed\nmetadata. Exclude only transient build caches. Also back up the deployment's\npassword-hash configuration separately.\n\nRestore into an empty instance path while the runner is stopped, preserve file\npermissions, then start it with the same `OMNIHARNESS_ROOT` and\n`OMNIHARNESS_INSTANCE`. The auth key is required to read encrypted settings and\nvalidate existing sessions. If it is intentionally omitted, rotate the\npassword and expect every client to authenticate again.\n\nClient profile lists and platform-secure bearer sessions are client state, not\npart of a runner backup.\n\n## Disposable smoke check\n\nThis uses an isolated root and a hidden prompt. The password is not passed as a\ncommand-line argument or printed:\n\n```bash\nsmoke_root=\"$(mktemp -d \"${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/omniharness-smoke.XXXXXX\")\"\ntrap 'test -n \"$smoke_root\" && rm -rf -- \"$smoke_root\"' EXIT\nread -r -s -p \"Temporary runner password: \" smoke_password\nprintf '\\n'\nexport OMNIHARNESS_AUTH_PASSWORD=\"$smoke_password\"\nunset smoke_password\nOMNIHARNESS_ROOT=\"$smoke_root\" \\\nOMNIHARNESS_INSTANCE=smoke \\\npnpm runner --host 127.0.0.1 --port 3059 --no-static\n```\n\nIn another terminal, check liveness with:\n\n```bash\ncurl --fail --silent --show-error http://127.0.0.1:3059/api/healthz\n```\n\nPress Ctrl-C in the runner terminal. The trap removes only the temporary root\ncreated by this command.\n"
  }

    "text": "# OmniHarness\n\nOmniHarness is a local control plane for supervising ACP-backed coding agents.\nOne logical headless runner owns SQLite, auth, supervision, PTYs, and agent\nprocesses; the shared Vite interface runs in the web/PWA, Electron, iOS,\nAndroid, and VS Code and can stay connected to multiple runners.\n\nUse it when you want one durable place to start coding-agent runs, watch worker output, recover conversations, inspect execution events, and keep local agent processes behind a clear supervisory layer.\n\n## What You Get\n\n- **Multi-agent supervision:** start implementation, planning, and direct-control conversations with supported ACP workers.\n- **Live run visibility:** stream messages, worker output, execution events, and status changes while a run is active.\n- **Durable local history:** persist runs, messages, workers, settings, auth records, and execution events in SQLite.\n- **CLI parity:** launch and watch the same conversation modes from the terminal.\n- **ACP server mode:** expose OmniHarness itself as an ACP agent over stdio for compatible clients.\n- **Managed agent environment:** spawn workers with a practical `PATH` even when the app starts from a GUI, editor, or service manager.\n- **Phone-friendly local UI:** run the web app as a local PWA for supervising work away from the terminal.\n- **Multi-runner clients:** save any number of authenticated runners, keep their\n  event streams live, and switch the visible workspace without reconnecting.\n\n## Project Status\n\nOmniHarness is early open-source software under active development. Expect sharp edges, fast-moving internals, and occasional database or workflow changes. The core local loop is the priority: reliable worker launch, observable agent activity, durable recovery, and straightforward developer setup.\n\n## Install On macOS\n\nThe supported release path is a Mac with `git`, `curl`, and Terminal. Clone the\nrepository and run the launcher:\n\n```bash\ngit clone https://github.com/danduma/omniharness.git\ncd omniharness\n./omniharness\n```\n\nThat one command installs and starts the server and production UI together. It:\n\n1. selects a supported Node version (`>=22.13 <26`);\n2. installs the repository's pnpm version and dependencies;\n3. installs the maintained Codex ACP adapter and Codex CLI from published npm\n   packages, with no ACP source build;\n4. builds the production Vite interface when its inputs change; and\n5. starts OmniHarness and opens [http://localhost:3050](http://localhost:3050).\n\nOn first start, choose a web login password or press Enter to generate one. A\ngenerated password is printed once; save it before continuing.
